div.p: The tribes of the deep and the far-scattered ranks of fish of every kind, the swimming race of Amphitrite, I will declare, Antoninus, supreme power upon the earth; all that the billowy flood holds, and where each has its pasture, their watery weddings and watery broods, the life of fishes, their enmities and their loves, their counsels too, and the cunning, many-sided craft of the gainful art of the sea, all that men have devised against the unspeaking fish; they sail the dim sea with daring heart, and have looked upon depths not to be looked upon, and by their arts portioned out the measures of the brine, men more than mortal. The mountain boar and the bear the hunter sees, and watches them as they meet him in the open, to strike from afar and master at close quarters; and both upon firm earth the beast and the man do battle, while the hounds, companions and leaders, mark out the quarry and guide on their masters to the very lair, and follow near as helpers. For these no winter brings such fear, nor does the heat of harvest breed fever; for many are the hunters' refuges, shady thickets and ridges and caves of self-roofing rock; and many silver rivers stretch along the hills, ever-flowing stewards, a cure for thirst and for bathing; and beside the green-bordered streams the lowly grasses lie, a soft couch to take calm sleep after toil, and to eat the seasonable supper of the country woodland, the many things that grow upon the hills. Delight attends the chase more than the sweat. And those who arm destruction against the birds— for them too the prey is easy and within sight: some they plunder from the nest as they slumber, in secret; some they draw down with lime-bearing reeds; and others fall of themselves into the long-woven snares, in want of a resting-place, and meet a joyless lodging. But for the toil-enduring fishermen the contests are uncertain, and hope, unstable, fawns upon the mind like a dream; for they do not strive upon the unmoving land, but ever with the cold and uncontrollably raging water are they thrown together, which even to look upon from land brings dread, and to test with the eyes alone; on small timbers, servants of the storm-winds, wandering, and ever holding their spirit among the surges, ever they watch the violet cloud, and ever they tremble at the darkening path of the brine; no shelter from the roving winds, no defence against the rains, no guard against the harvest fire do they carry. And besides, the grim, ill-seen terrors of the grim deep, the sea-monsters, they shudder at, that meet them whenever they cross the sanctuary of the under-sea; no pack of hounds leads the sea-road for the harpooners; for the tracks are invisible to swimmers, nor do they see where the fish, meeting them, will come near for the catch—for it travels by no single road; in feeble hairs and the bent lips of bronze, in reeds and lines they have their strength. Yet you lack nothing of delight, if you should wish to take your pleasure, and sweet is the royal sport of the chase. A ship, well-bolted, well-benched, exceeding light, the young men drive with hurrying oars, beating the back of the sea; and the best steersman at the stern brings the steady, faultless ship to a wide sea-room, purpling and calm; there, the countless tribes of feasting fishes are fed, which the servants ever tend, fattening them with abundant food, a most ready chorus for the chase for you, blessed one, and for your great-glorying son, the flocks of the hunt. For straightway from your hand you send into the sea the well-twisted line, and swiftly the fish, meeting it, takes the bronze barb upon its jaw, and quickly is drawn from the king's hand, not unwilling, and your heart is gladdened, lord of the earth; for great is the delight to eyes and to mind, to behold the fish, fettered, quivering and writhing. But be gracious to me, you who are king over the sea's pathway, the wide-ruling son of Cronos, the earth-holder, and Sea herself, and you dwellers in the loud-roaring sea, gods, vouchsafe me to tell of your herds and sea-nurtured tribes; and may you, lady Goddess, guide each thing aright, and to the father and the son of the all-ruling king prepare these welcome gifts of your song. Countless indeed and beyond reckoning are the tribes that move swimming in the depths of the sea; these no man could name with exactness, for none has reached the sea's furthest bound; but only to about three hundred fathoms do men know and have looked upon Amphitrite. Much—for boundless and immeasurably deep is the sea— lies hidden, things no mortal man could tell of, unseen as they are; small is the mind of men, and small their strength. For I do not think the brine of the all-mothering earth nurtures fewer herds or lesser tribes; but whether the breed be matched in both, or whether one outstrips the other, the gods know clearly, and we with the thoughts of men may take our measure. For fishes their kind and their habits and their path in the brine are appointed, nor are the pastures the same for all the swimming tribes: some graze along the low-lying shores, feeding on the sand and what grows in the sands— the hippus, the swift cuckoo-fish, the yellow erythrini, the citharus, the red mullet, and the feeble melanuri, the schools of horse-mackerel, the sole and the broad-tailed slender ribbon-fish, and the mormyrus, that nimble fish, the mackerel and carp and those that love the shores. Others again in the mud and the shallows of the sea are fed: the rays and the monstrous broods of the ox-ray, the troublesome sting-ray and the cramp-fish, truly named, the turbot and the cod and the gurnards and the works of the hake, the lizard-fish and the weevers and all that are bred in the mud. And along the leek-green sand, beneath the green herbage, the sprats and the goat-fish and the silver-fish graze, the picarel and the blenny and the sea-bream, and both kinds of bogue, and all to whom it is dear to feed about the seaweed. The grey mullets again, and the cephali, the most righteous race of the brine, the bass and the bold-hearted bonito and the chremetes, the pelamyds, the conger-eels, and the one they call the slippery one, ever dwell in the sea that neighbours the rivers or the lagoons, where sweet water gives the brine a rest, and a great muddy outpouring is mingled in, drawn down by the eddies from the land; there they feed on the lovely fare and grow fat in the sweet brine. The bass too does not stay outside the very rivers, but swims up from the sea into the river-mouths; and the eels from the rivers come down to the flats of the sea. The sea-girt rocks are of many kinds: some are soaked with weed, and much moss grows about them; these the perch and the rainbow-wrasse and the channus feed about, the saupe among them, with mottled backs, the slender thrushes and the wrasses, those that the fishermen have named with the name of a soft-minded man. Other rocks, low-lying, near the sandy sea, are scaly crags, which the cirrhis and the sow-fish and the basilisks, and among them the millers and the rosy tribes of the mullet, haunt. And other rocks, green-fronted with grass upon their wet brows, hold the sargue as a dweller, and the maigre, the chalceus and the corvina, named for its dusky hue, and the parrot-wrasse, which alone among all the voiceless fish utters a wet babbling, and alone sends its food back again up its mouth, to feast on it a second time, chewing the cud like sheep. And all the rocks that are thick with cockles or with limpets, where there are chambers and lairs for the fish to enter, there the braize abide and the shameless wild-braize, the cercurus and the gluttons and the loathsome morays and the lizard-fish and the late-dying race of the orphos, which more than all linger longest upon the land alive, and even when cut still gasp beneath the iron. Others abide deep down beneath the waves in their dens—the sheep-fish and the hepatus and the prepontes, mighty and great in growth, but sluggishly they wind their ways; therefore they never leave their gully, but there in ambush wait by their cranny for whatever may draw near, bringing unseen doom upon the weaker fish; among them is the hake also, who beyond all cowers at the harvest Dog-star's bitter onset, and stays sunk in his dark recess, nor before comes forth, for as long a time as the fierce star blows. There is a fish that haunts the wave-washed rocks, yellow to look upon, in form like to the mullets, which some of men call the adonis, and others have named the exocoetus, because outside the sea it makes its bed, and alone passes onto the dry land, of all that have gills, those folds of the mouth, on either side. For when calm lulls the works of the bright sea to rest, then, borne in upon the rushing breakers, it stretches itself upon the rocks and takes calm sleep. But it dreads the race of sea-birds, who are its foes; and if it spies one drawing near, it leaps like a dancer, that the swell of the sea, rolling it onward, may save it from the crags. And some feed both among the rocks and in the sands— the gilthead, named for its splendour, and the weevers, the snub-nosed grey-fish and the valiant dentex, the darting scorpion-fish, a twofold race, and both kinds of the long sphyraenae, and with them the slender needle-fish; and there is the charax, and the light tumblers, the gobies; and there is the grievous race of the sea-mice, who beyond all are bold among the swimmers, and stand against men, though they are not so great; relying chiefly on a hard hide and on the close-set teeth within, they fight with fishes and with men more mighty than themselves. Others have their roaming in the measureless seas, far from the dry land, nor are they comrades of the shores— the tunnies, darting, in fishes pre-eminent in onset, swiftest of all, and the sword-fish, truly named, and the monstrous race of the orcynus, and the premades and the cybeae, the coliae and the cudgel-fish and the broods of the dolphin-fish. Among these too is the beauty-fish, well-named, a sacred fish; and among them dwells the pilot-fish, which the sailors revere, and have given it the name of the convoy of ships; for, rejoicing exceedingly in the ships that run through the wet, they follow as convoys, fellow-voyagers, one here, another there, leaping all about the well-benched chariot of the sea, on both its sides and about the stern-rudders of the steering-oars, and others gather about the prow; nor would you say their voyaging was of their own will, but under a bond, fast bound, as it were, to the well-bolted planks, drawn against their will, led on by necessity. So great a love gathers the swarm to the hollow ships. As when a city-bearing king, or some man that has won the prize, his head crowned with fresh garlands, the boys and the youths and the men attending lead up into his house, and ever throng about him, until he passes over the well-fenced threshold of his halls; so these ever follow the swift-faring ships, so long as no fear of land drives them; but when they mark the dry land, and greatly loathe the firm-set field, again they set off all together and, as from a starting-post, all leap away, and no longer follow the ships. This is a true sign for sailors that land is near, when they see them leaving their fellow-voyagers. Pilot-fish, honoured in seafaring, by you a man divines that gentle breezes of the winds will come; for in fair weather you set out, and fair-weather signs you show. And in the open sea likewise the ship-holder is your companion; it is long to look upon, a cubit in length, dusky in hue, and its form is like the eels', and the sharp mouth of its head bends downward and is curved, like to the point of a rounded hook. A marvel of the slippery ship-holder the sailors have noted; yet no man, hearing it, would believe it in his heart; for ever the mind of untried men is hard to convince, nor will they trust even what is true: a ship straining under the rush of a violent wind, running with sails spread through the measures of the brine, the fish, gaping a little, holds back from below, forcing it wholly under the keel; no longer does it cleave the wave even when it strives, but stands fast and firm, as though shut up within unbuffeted harbours. And all its sails fall slack about the forestays, the ropes groan, the yard-arm bows, driven by the gust, and upon the stern all the helm-ropes the steersman lets go, urging on the path of the brine; but she neither minds the rudders nor obeys the winds, nor is driven by the waves, but fixed fast she stays against her will, and even in her haste is fettered, rooted to the mouth of a worthless fish; and the sailors tremble, beholding the unseen bonds of the sea, and gaze upon a wonder like a dream. As when in the thickets a hunter, watching a swift-running deer, with the tip of an arrow strikes its limb and binds it from its course beneath the feathered shaft; and the deer, for all its haste, fixed by constraining pains, against its will awaits the bold hunter; such a fetter the nimble fish, meeting her, casts about the ship; and from such deeds it won its name. The chalcides too and the shads and the bream are borne in shoals, now along one sea-path, now another, whether about the rocks or in the open, or they run along the long shores, ever changing their strange road like wanderers. The pastures of the anthiae are chiefly in the deep rocks, their kindred; but they are not ever at home there, but stray everywhere, where their jaw, where their belly and ravenous, insatiable love of food may bid; for beyond all others a greedy frenzy drives them, though they have a toothless space beneath the mouth. Four great-bulked tribes of the anthiae graze: the yellow and the white, and the third blood-dark; others they call the fair-eyed and the auloposes, because for these, coiling above in a circle, a dark, encompassing brow is set as a crown. Two, fencing their fitted limbs with hard shells, swim in the bosoms of the sea— the spike-shelled crawfish and the lobster; and these both dwell among the rocks and feed among the rocks. The lobster, beyond all telling, hides in its heart a love for its own chamber unspeakable, nor ever leaves it willingly, but if any by force has dragged it and, carrying it far elsewhere, lets it go again into the sea, yet it, not long after, returns to its own gully, hastening, nor will it choose another, strange recess, nor sets itself upon another rock, but seeks out both the home it left and its haunts and the pasture of that brine which nourished it, and did not loathe the sea from which the sea-faring hunters made it a stranger. So then even for swimming things their own home and the sea of their fathers and the place of their hearth, where they were born, drops sweet gladness into the heart; nor is fatherland sweetest of all to ephemeral mortals only; nor is there anything more grievous and more wretched than for one whom necessity makes spend a painful, city-exiled life far from his country, a stranger among aliens, dragging the yoke of dishonour. In that kindred are the crabs also, the wanderers, and the pastures of the prawns and the shameless tribes of the pagurus, who too have a portion numbered among the amphibious. All those whose legs are set beneath a shell slough off the older shell, and another beneath rises up from the nethermost flesh; and the paguri, when they perceive the force of the breaking case, crave everywhere, hungering for food, that the parting of the shell may come more easily when they are full; and when the broken fence has slipped away, they at first are stretched out upon the sands just so, mindful neither of food nor of aught else, thinking themselves to be among the dead, and no longer to breathe warm breath, and they tremble in their thin new-grown hide; but afterwards, gathering their wits again, taking a little courage, they feed upon the sand; till then they have a helpless spirit, faint, until about their limbs the new covering grows hard. As a physician tending a disease-burdened man in the first days keeps him fasting from food, blunting the fierce force of the malady, but then offers him a little nourishment as he sickens, until he purges all the ruin and the limb-gnawing miseries and the pains; so they spring up in their new-grown cases, fearing to escape the evil dooms of disease. Other crawling things dwell in the sea's channels— the crooked octopus and the cordylus, and the centipede-fish, hateful to fishermen, and the osmylus; and these too are amphibious; and once a country man, a tiller of the soil, busy with planting near the sea, saw an osmylus or an octopus twined about the fruitful boughs, eating the sweet fruit of the plants. And like portion to these crawling things has the crafty cuttlefish; and other shell-skinned tribes are in the waves, many among the rocks, and some feed in the sands— the nerites and the race of trumpet-shells and the purple-fish themselves, the whelks and the mussels and—truly named—the razor-shell, the dewy oysters and the jagged sea-urchins; these, if a man cut them even small in pieces and into the sea cast them, grow together again and live again and feed. But the hermit-crabs themselves have no shell grown from birth, but naked and uncovered and feeble are they born, and they contrive themselves acquired houses, casting a borrowed covering about their soft limbs; for when they spy a shell left orphaned just so, its dweller departed and its hearth deserted, they dive within and, beneath alien cases, sitting, they dwell, and the dwelling they have won; with it they crawl, and within carry the fence about, whether the nerites left the covering or the whelk or the trumpet-shell; but the entrances of trumpet-shells they love most, because they are wide to abide in and light to carry. But when, growing, the hermit-crab has filled the recess where it dwells within, it no longer keeps that house, but leaving it seeks a wider hollow of a shell to cast about it. And often about a snug little shell among the hermit-crabs a struggle and great strife arises, and, driving the other out, the stronger casts about herself the fitting house she has won. There is a fish covered with a hollow shell, in form like the octopuses, which they call the nautilus, famed for its own seafaring; it dwells in the sands, and rises to the top of the water face down, that the sea may not fill it; but when it has floated up over the billows of Amphitrite, straightway turning over it sails, like a man skilled with the boat: two feet above, like cables, it raises up, and between flows, like a sail, a thin membrane, and is stretched out to the wind; while below two, touching the brine, like to the steering-oars, are pilots and guide the house and the ship and the fish. But when it dreads an evil near at hand, no longer to the winds does it flee entrusting itself, but draws in all its tackle, sails and rudders, and at once takes in the wave within, and, weighed down, is dragged under by the rush of the water. Ah, whoever first found out the ships, the chariots of the sea, whether some immortal contrived it, or some man, daring, first prayed to cross the wave, surely, looking upon that voyaging, he fashioned the timber-fitted work in the likeness of the fish's deed: some things he spread to the breezes from the forestays, and others behind as steering-tackle for the ships. The sea-monsters, mighty-limbed, prodigious, the wonders of the deep, laden with irresistible strength, a terror to all eyes that look on them, ever armed with deadly madness, many of them are turned about in the wide-pathed seas, there where the unmarked watch-posts of Poseidon are, and few come near the breakers, only such as the shores bear, heavy-roaring, and that do not leave the brine; of these are the chill lion and the grim hammerhead, the deadly leopards and the spouting physaloi; and there is the black, furious race of the tunnies, and there the blood-red saw-fish, and the ill-met gapings of the cruel lamna, and the maltha, named not for any soft feeblenesses, the troublesome rams and the abominable burden of the hyena, and the shameless, ravening dog-sharks; and among the dog-sharks the breed is threefold: one, wild, in the seas is numbered among the deadly monsters; other tribes, two, whirl among the mightiest fishes in the deep mud: one, by the black spines, are named, fitly, the spined; another, together with them, are called dog-fish; and of the dog-fish there are diverse tribes, the pups and the smooth ones and the prickly; and among them the angel-sharks and the foxes and the spotted ones; and like deeds they all have, and feed their fare among one another. The dolphins delight in the loud-resounding shores and dwell in the seas, and never is the sea without dolphins; for about them Poseidon shows great love; because, when he sought the dark-eyed maiden, daughter of Nereus, Amphitrite, who fled from his bed, the dolphins, marking her, in the halls of Ocean hidden, brought him word; and straightway the dark-haired god seized the maiden, refusing him, and subdued her. And her he made his consort, queen of the sea, and he blessed his kindly servants for their message, and in his own domain gave them surpassing honour. There are among the pitiless monsters some that even outside the brine come forth upon the life-giving dry land; long upon the shores and the fields beside the sea the eels mingle, and the shielded turtle, and the deadly castor-beasts, of grievous mourning, who upon the shingle pour out an ill-boding, mournful cry to men; and whoever takes into his ears that painful voice and hears the wail of that loathsome clamour, he shall not be far from death soon, but for him that most dreadful voice prophesies ruin and doom. Yes, and they say the shameless whale of the sea comes out onto the dry land and warms itself in the sun. The seals by night ever leave the sea, and often by day, among the rocks and the sands, quiet they abide and take their sleep out of the water. Father Zeus, in you are all things and from you are they rooted; whether you dwell in the highest house of the upper air, or everywhere—for to a mortal it is impossible to tell. With what love did you separate and scatter apart the gleaming upper air and the lower air and the streaming water and the all-mothering earth, each from the other, yet all in one another, under the bond of unbreakable concord you bound them, and by necessity pressed them, unshaken, under a common yoke; for neither is the upper air without the lower, nor the air without water, nor again is water made without earth, but in one another they grow, and all go one road, and unwind one cycle of exchange. Therefore also they are hostages to common broods, the amphibious; and some come up upon the land from the sea, while others again through the air mingle with Amphitrite—the light gulls and the wailing tribes of the halcyons, and the mighty sea-eagles, the ravishers, and all else that fishes and sets upon the watery hunt. And again the air they cleave, sea-creatures though they are, the flying-squids and the race of sea-hawks and the deep-sea swallow; these, when they fear a stronger fish near at hand, leap up out of the sea and fly through the air. But some both far and high let go their wing— the squids, which you might think a bird and not a fish to look upon, when in shoals they rush to fly; and beneath them the swallows have their path; and the hawks hover close above the very brine, just grazing the surface of the sea, so much that, to look upon, both are alike to swimmers and to fliers. These are, as it were, the cities among fishes, and these the companies that are sundered apart of the sea-roving breed. Of them some stray together in crowds, the nimble tribes, like flocks or armies, those that are called gregarious; others again in rows; and some are like ambush-bands or companies of ten; and one goes alone, apart from the rest, setting off in solitude; and others pass two by two; and some abide there in their own chambers. In winter all of them dread exceedingly the eddies of the storm-winds, dread the swell of the ill-sounding sea itself; for beyond all others the fishy broods shudder at their own dear sea when it rages; then some, having heaped up the sand with their fins, cower beneath it, helpless; others, beneath the rocks huddling together, dive in shoals; and some flee to the deepest seas, down to the inmost abyss; for those neither roll over too much, nor by the winds are they whirled up from the bottom, nor does any blast rush through to the sea's lowest root; and the great depth keeps from them the chilling pains and the harsh onset of winter. But when the flowery seasons of spring upon the earth laugh with their purple, and the sea breathes again, growing fair after winter, and grows calm, heaving gently, then the fishes from this side and that come thronging in all haste, rejoicing, near the land. As when, having fled the cloud of all-destroying war, a happy city, dear to the immortals, which long the all-bronze storm of foes flooded over, late ceasing at last and breathing again from the strife, gladly rejoices and in the labours of peace delights, sweet labours, and feasts in fair weather, filled with men and with the dance-beat of women; so they, having gladly fled the grievous toils and the shivering of the sea, exulting over the brine, leaping, rush about like dancers. And in spring the sweet sting of compelling Aphrodite and weddings come to their prime, and the loves of one another for all, both those that throng the life-giving earth and those in the bosoms of the air and those that range the loud-roaring sea. And in spring most of all the race of the swimmers do the goddesses of birth, the Eileithyiae, release from the heavy pangs of egg-bearing. For the females, in want of brood and of birth, press their slender bellies upon the sands; for not easily do they part, but the eggs are held fast together within the womb, grown confusedly into one; and how should they bear them all at once? Straitened by pains, they hardly bring forth their brood. So the Fates have given no easy birth to fishes either, nor are pangs for earthly women alone, but everywhere the Eileithyiae are burdensome. Of the males, again, some bringing dooms upon the fish, feasters, hasten and draw near to the breakers; others run on ahead, pursued behind by the female herds, since, drawn by the love of mating, they hasten after the males with uncontrollable rush. There some, rubbing their bellies upon one another, shed the liquid seed behind, and the females, eager with desire, with greedy mouths gulp it down; by such a wedding are they filled with spawn. This is the most common law among fishes; but some too have beds and chambers and wives apart, set separately, having mated; for great among fishes is Aphrodite, and Frenzy and Jealousy, that heavy god, and all that hot Love begets, when he stirs riotous revel in the heart. And many, parting, for the sake of the bed do battle, like suitors, who about a bride gather in numbers and, well-matched, contend in wealth and splendour; but these things fishes have not, but strength and jaws and the jagged fence of teeth within— with these they strive and arm themselves for the wedding; and whoever wins the throw among them, with victory at once finds the wedding. And some take their delight in many wedded mates—the race of the sargues and the dusky merle; others love and cherish a single bedfellow, the canthari and the Aetnaean fish, and rejoice not in many. But not like the eels, nor like the turtles, nor like the octopuses, is the manner of wedding, nor like the black moray's, but they have a way of mating turned aside from the bed: for the eels, poured coil within coil into one another, turn their wet bodies in thick array, twining together, and from them there drips, like to foam, an ichor, and it is hidden in the sands; and the mud receiving it conceives, and brings forth the coils of eels. Such too is the birth of the slippery congers. But the turtles greatly fear and loathe their wedding; for to them it is not desirable, as to others, the delight of the bed, but they have far more pain; for very hard is the goad in the males toward love, an unyielding bone, whetted for the joyless bed. Therefore they fight, and with their curving teeth tear one another, when they meet at close quarters, the females shunning the rough wedding, the males longing, willing, for the bed of the unwilling, until by force one, victorious, yokes her in compelled love, like a captive, the prize of war. Like the deeds of the bed are those of land dogs and of sea-turtles; like too those of seals; for very long each pair behind are joined together, fastened as by a bond. But the octopus has deadly weddings, and bitter ruin goes with it, a common end of death and of the bed; for it does not before abstain from love, nor cease, before its strength fails from its weakening limbs, and itself, falling helpless in the sands, perishes; for all devour it, whoever come near, the cowardly hermit-crabs and the crabs and other fishes, which before it itself easily devoured as it crept upon them; beneath them, alive though it still be, lying just so, in no way defending itself, it is carved up, until it dies. By such a joyless love-doom does it perish. And likewise the female too, labouring with birth-pangs, perishes; for not for them, as for others, do the eggs leap out separately, but, fastened to one another in clusters, hardly do they pass through the narrow channel. Therefore the octopuses never live beyond the measure of a single year; for they ever waste away with most dreadful weddings and most dreadful births. And about the moray a tale goes, not unclear, how a serpent weds her, and she comes out of the sea herself, eagerly, longing, to the longing partner of the wedding. Indeed the bitter viper, sharpened within by fiery madness, raves toward love and is drawn near the shore, and quickly spies a hollow rock, and there spits out its deadly venom, and all the bitter rancour of its teeth it spews forth, its fierce wrath, the treasure of ruin, that gentle and serene it may come to the wedding. Standing then upon the shore it hisses its own tune, calling for love; and swiftly the black moray hears the cry and rushes, faster than an arrow. She from the sea strains forth, while he from the land steps upon the grey breakers of the sea; and both, eager to meet one another, fall together, and the bride, panting, took the viper's head into her gaping mouth; and rejoicing in the wedding, she goes back again to the sea, to her haunts, while him the land draws by his coil, and again he laps up the chill venom he had let go before and drained from his teeth. But if he does not find that rancour again, which a wayfarer, seeing him truly, washed away with rushing water, then in vexation he flings his body about, until he takes the lot of a wretched, unlooked-for death, ashamed that, weaponless in the arms he had trusted, he, a serpent, was; and on the rock he destroyed both his body and himself by the venom. The dolphins make their wedding even as men do, and brace their members all like to men's; nor is the male's passage ever visible, but within it is hidden, and is drawn out for the bed's need. Such are the loves among fishes, and such the beds. Different fishes long for the bed in different seasons, and bring forth their kind: to some it is summer, to some winter, to some spring, or waning autumn shows their birth. And most in a single year labour with one brood, the most of them; but the bass is burdened twice by the Eileithyiae; and the red mullets are named for their threefold births; the scorpion-fish again bears its barb at four travails; and to the carps alone are five broods; and of the hake alone they say none has ever marked the kind, but this even now remains unseen among men. And when, full of the spring-time spawn, the egg-laying fishes are, some, each in his own place, abide quietly in their own homes; but many, gathering, set forth on a common road to the Euxine Sea, that there they may bear their young. For that gulf is sweeter than all Amphitrite, watered by boundless and fair-flowing rivers, and soft and sandy are its sheltering bays; and in it are well-grown pastures and waveless shores and hollow rocks and muddy clefts and shady headlands and all that is dearest to fishes; and in it neither any monster hostile nor any plague destructive to the swimmers is bred, nor any of those that are foes to the smaller fishes, the coils of octopuses, nor lobsters nor crabs; few are the dolphins, and feebler even they than the monster breed, and harmless they range about. Therefore to the fishes that water is exceedingly welcome, and greatly they hasten to go there. And they set forth all together in companies, one here, another there, gathering into one, and one is the road for all of them, the convoy and the rush and again the home-returning surge. The dappled swarms accomplish the Thracian Bosporus and the Bebrycian sea besides, and the strait mouth of the Pontus, crossing the long course of Amphitrite. As when from the Ethiopians and the streams of Egypt the high-flying choir of clamorous cranes comes, fleeing the snowy crag of Atlas and the winter and the feeble broods of the puny Pygmies; and as they fly in rows their wide swarms shadow the air and hold an unbroken furrow; so then the myriad-tribed ranks of the sea cleave the great wave of the Euxine; and the sea grows full, shuddering thick, lashed with their fins, until, hastening, they rest from their long expedition and from birth. But when the measure of autumn passes by, they bethink them of return, since, colder than other seas, winter drives hard upon that eddying brine; for it is not deep, and is easily buffeted by the winds, which beat upon it, overweening and deadly. Therefore, shunning the Amazonian lagoon, again with their young they are borne back homeward, and scatter over the sea, where each shall feed. But all that are called soft-fleshed, those whose make of limbs is bloodless and boneless, and all the tribes that are covered with close scales, or with horny plates fenced about—these, like the others, have care of egg-bearing pangs; but from the ravenous dog-shark and the eagle-ray and all the tribes that are called cartilaginous, and from the fish-feeding kings, the dolphins, and the ox-eyed seal, straightway the young from birth come forth in the likeness of their parents. And indeed all that dwell in the sea that are live-bearing love and tend their offspring, but nothing more godlike than the dolphins has been made; for in truth they were once men and dwelt in cities together with mortals, but by the will of Dionysus they exchanged the land for the sea and put on the form of fishes; yet even now the righteous spirit of men within them preserves the human mind and human deeds. For when the twofold brood of their travail comes to the light, straightway, as soon as they are born, about their own mother they swim and frolic and dart within her teeth and linger beneath the mother's mouth; and she with loving-kindness holds herself up and about her young turns gladdening and exceedingly exulting. And she offers her breast to both, one to each, to suck the sweet milk; for the god gave her both milk and a nature of breasts like to women's. So then for a while she has care of such nursing; but when they come to their strength, straightway for them the mother goes down as a guide upon the road of the chase at their desire, and teaches them the hunting of fish, nor before stands far from her young, nor leaves them, until their limbs have grown to fullness and to strength, but ever near, overseeing keepers, they follow. Such a wonder you might marvel at in your heart, and lovely delight, when sailing you behold in a temperate breeze, watching, or in a calm, the comely herds of the dolphins, the darling of the brine; for in front, in throngs, like boys, the young go, the new brood, like those of a dance, changing the manifold, intricately-wheeling circle; and behind, great and pre-eminent, not apart from their young, come the guardian host, even as to the tender feeding lambs the shepherds follow in spring. As when from the works of the Muses the children go in throngs, and behind them as overseers near follow the elders, censors of modesty and of mind and of sense; for fitting old age makes a man righteous; so then the dolphins too, parents to their young, follow, lest any unkind thing should meet them. Yes, and the seal too tends her offspring no worse; for she also has breasts, and in her breasts are streams of milk; but for her not amid the waves but upon the dry land is the labour of the womb released as she comes up, the timely pang; and she abides all twelve days with her young there upon the dry land; but on the thirteenth, with the dawn, holding her new-grown cubs in her arms, she dives into the sea, glorying in her young, as though showing them their fatherland. As when a woman in a foreign land, having borne a child, gladly comes to her own country and her own home, carrying the child all day long in her arms, showing him the house, her mother's haunt, and fondly embraces him, an insatiable delight; and he, though understanding not each thing, gazes about, at the hall and all the haunts of his parents; so then that sea-beast too brings her own brood to the sea and shows them the works of the deep. Gods, then, not in men alone are children dearest, and sweeter than the light and than life, but also in birds and pitiless beasts and flesh-eating fishes a helpless, self-taught, keen longing for offspring is bred; and for their young to die and to fill up all wretched misery they are ready, not unwilling, eager. Already one upon the hills has marked a deep-roaring lion, the hunter, standing over his young, fighting for his own kind; nor does he reck of the thick stones that fly, nor of the javelin, but just so keeps his fearless courage and might, though stricken and torn by every cast; nor before he dies does he draw back, but over his young, half-dead, he strides on, and he cares not for death so much as that he may not see his young by the hunters shut up in their own self-made den, the den of beasts. Already by the whelp-nursing bed of a new-littered bitch a shepherd, drawing near, even if he was a friend before, has withdrawn, fearing the mother's baying wrath, how she guards her young, nor knows any shame, but is dreadful for all to approach. As about their stolen calves the cows, in grief, not far from the wailings of women, groan their lamentations, and afflict the very herdsmen; and a man has heard the unceasing wail of the ospray at dawn about her young, or of the shrill-voiced nightingale, or has come near in spring to the swallows mourning their young, which men cruel or serpents have stolen from them out of the nest. Among fishes, again, the dolphin is foremost in love of its young; yet others too tend their kind. A marvel is this of the sea-roving dog-shark: by her follow her new-sprung young, and to them the mother is a shield; but when they are afraid—and boundless are the terrors in the sea—then she takes her young within her flanks, into the very entrance, the very road, whence they slipped at their birth; and such a labour, suffering it though she does, she gladly endures, and again pours her young beneath into her bowels, and lets them out again, when they breathe free of fear. Such defence too the angel-shark provides for her young, but for her there is no entering the belly, as for the dog-sharks, but in her sides are clefts on either hand beneath the fins, like the jaws of other fishes, in which she shelters the terror of her frightened young. Others again receive their frightened young through the mouth and rescue them, as into a house or a den; even so the glaucus, who beyond all loves its young of all that are egg-layers among the fishes; for he abides, sitting by, until they are born, the young beneath the eggs, and ever swims beside them; and when he sees them in fear of a stronger fish, gaping he takes them in through his mouth, until the terror withdraws, and then again he spits them forth from his throat. But than the tunny I think no fish more lawless, nor one gone further in evil-mindedness, dwells in the brine; for when she has borne her eggs, and fled the heavy pang, she herself, who bore them, devours all she can find, pitiless, who eats her own young, still ignorant of flight, nor does any pity for her own birth come over her. There are some that neither by weddings are begotten nor by births are born, self-completed and self-made broods, the oysters all, which are bred in the very mud; of these there is neither any female kind, nor in exchange any males, but all are of one stock and all alike. So too the feeble nation of the puny anchovy springs from no blood and from no parents; for when from the clouds the mind of Zeus draws up the rain violent over the sea and beyond restraint, at once all the sea, mingled with eddies and back-blowing gusts, hisses and foams and stands swelling up, and they, in unmarked and unseen weddings, all together both came to be and were nourished and appeared, in myriads, feeble, a hoary race; and from their birth they are called by name, fitly, the spawn-of-foam. Others spring from the muddy surge; for when in the eddies and the back-flowings of the sea the all-confused refuse is churned up by the wind rushing on, then all the dank mud gathers together into one going, and when the calm is spread, forthwith the sand and the unspeakable refuse of the sea rot, and from them spring up creatures past telling, like to maggots. There is no other race made feebler than the wretched anchovy; and to all the swimmers it is good fare; and they lick each other's bodies, one another's; and this is their food and their living; but when these throng the sea all together, seeking out either a shadowed rock or the recesses of the sea and a refuge in the deep, then all the grey-green Amphitrite turns white. As when the swift might of the evening Zephyr shadows the wide threshing-floor with snowflakes, and nothing of the dark earth shows beneath to look upon, but all is white, covered with snow ever-falling; so then, filled full with the boundless shoals, the silvery threshing-floor of Poseidon appears all white.

Thus do the fish-fed pastures and the tribes of the sea roam; in such a wedding, in such a birth they take delight; and all these things some one of the immortals revealed to men; for what can mortals accomplish without the gods? Not so much as to lift the print of a foot, nor so much as to open wide the bright orbs of their eyes; but the gods themselves rule and direct all things, being near while far away; and unshaken necessity it is to obey; this neither strength nor any force can escape, having haughtily wrenched with its rough jaws, like a colt that spits out the bit; but ever the most exalted blessed ones turn the reins wherever they will, and one follows like a man of sound mind, before with a harsh whip and against his will he is driven. They too gave to men the much-gainful arts to possess, and put all prudence into them. And each god was named for differing works, in which each took oversight and honour. Demeter brings the gift of the yoke of oxen and the ploughing of earth and the harvest of the fruitful wheat. But to fashion timbers and to raise up halls, and to work garments from the flowery fleece of sheep, Pallas taught the dwellers on earth; and the gifts of Ares are swords and the bronze tunics about the limbs and helmets and spears and all in which Enyo delights. And the gifts of the Muses and Apollo are songs. Hermes bestowed the assembly and the contests of strength. And to Hephaestus belongs the hammering sweat. And these thoughts of the sea also, and the achievement of the chase, and the multitude of the water-faring, a god gave to be marked out by men—he who first, filling up the riven hollows of the earth with the rivers gathered there, poured forth the bitter sea and crowned it round, fencing it about with brows and breakers, whether one should call him wide-ruling Poseidon, or ancient Nereus, or rather Phorcys, or some other guiding god of the sea. But may they all, as many gods as hold Olympus, and those of the sea, and those of the well-watered land, and those that dwell in the air, have all-gracious hearts to you, blessed sceptre-bearer, and to your bright-childed line, and to all peoples, and to our songs. Among fishes there is no reckoning of justice nor any shame, no love; for all of them swim hostile to one another, foes; and the stronger ever feasts on the weaker, and one swims upon another bringing doom, and one furnishes food for another. For some by their jaws and by valour overcome the weaker; some have venom in the mouth; for some the spines are grown to defend against deadly wounds, bitter and sharp, the points of fiery wrath. But to those to whom the god gave neither strength nor any sting whetted from their limbs, to them out of the mind he made a weapon, gainful counsel, full of devices, and these by guiles have often destroyed a strong and superior fish. Such is the medicine of defence that follows the cramp-fish, soft-skinned, self-taught, in its own limbs. For it is soft in body and altogether feeble and sluggish, weighed down with slowness, nor would you say, seeing it, that it swims; for very hard to discern is the path it winds, creeping through the grey water; but in its flanks the guile of its weakness is its strength: rays are grown along its sides on either hand, twofold; and if any draw near and touch them, straightway it quenched the strength of his limbs, and his blood is frozen, and he can no longer carry his limbs, but his force, as he slowly withers, is loosed by the senseless numbing. And she, well knowing what gift of the god she has received, lays back her body and waits among the sands; she lies unmoved, like a corpse; and whatever fish draws near to her flanks, that one is undone, and falls just so into a deep sleep of helplessness, fettered by his powerlessness; and she swiftly springs up, though she is not swift, rejoicing, and devours the living as though dead. And often in the deep, meeting fishes as they swim, she has quenched the swift onset of their haste, touching them near, and bound them in their rush; and they stand dry and helpless, mindful neither of their roads, the wretches, nor of flight; and she, abiding, devours them as they make no defence and have no feeling. As in the dark phantoms of dreams, when a man is terrified and longs to flee, his heart leaps, but his knees, as he quivers, are weighed down by an unshaken bond as he strains— such a limb-fetter the cramp-fish contrives for fishes. The fishing-frog again is a sluggish and soft fish alike, most foul to look upon; and its mouth opens exceeding wide; yet for it too craft has found fare for the belly. Itself, rolled in the dank mud, lies still, and stretches up a little fleshy fibre, which grows below from the tip of its lower jaw, thin and white, and its breath is foul; this it whirls often, a snare for the smaller fishes; and they, seeing it, rush to seize it. But it draws the fibre back quietly within, gently quivering, beneath its mouth, and they follow, suspecting nothing of the hidden snare, until unawares they are caught within the fishing-frog's wide jaws. As when a man, contriving a trap for the light birds, crumbles some grains before the doors of his snare, and puts others within, and sets up his device beneath; and longing for them, a keen desire of food draws them, and they come within, and no longer is return ready to slip out, but they have found an evil end to their feast; so does the feeble fishing-frog draw on those fishes, beguiling them, nor did they perceive it as they hastened to their own ruin. Such things too, I have heard, the crook-counselled vixen contrives: when she sees a thronging flock of birds, she lies down aslant, stretching her swift limbs, shuts her eyes, and closes her mouth altogether; you would say, looking on, that either she slept deep sleep, or truly lay a corpse; so breathless, plotting wily things, she is stretched out at full length; and they, seeing her, come straight on in throngs, the birds, and pluck at her fur with their feet, as if mocking; but when near her teeth they come, then, opening the doors of her snare, on a sudden she seized and snatched them, gaping wide, a gainful prey, as much as she took by her swoop. And indeed the crafty cuttlefish too has found a thievish hunt; for from its head are grown slender fronds, stretched forth, like tresses, with which it too, as with fishing-lines, draws fish for its hunting, lying face down in the sands, rolled beneath its shell. With those tresses too, when the waves rage in winter, it holds fast against the rocks, like a ship that has fastened its cables to the crags of the shore. The prawns are small to look upon, and their strength is small in their limbs, but by guiles they have destroyed even a valiant fish, the bass, famed for its own ravening greed. For these hasten and rush straight to seize the prawns, which have strength neither to flee nor to fight, but as they perish they destroy their slayers too. For when the bass gape and grip them within their teeth, these leap often and against the middle of the palate press their sharp horn, which rises for them from the top of the head; but the bass, sated with its dear prey, recks not of the prick; and it feeds and creeps on, until at last, worn out, doom takes it from its pains; and late it knows, slain by the corpse's barb. There is a flesh-eating ox that haunts the mud, broadest of all the fishes; for indeed its breadth has often been of eleven cubits or twelve; but worthless in strength, and its body has no share of valour, soft; and within are unseen teeth, small and not strong; by force it could subdue nothing, but by guile it takes and fetters even prudent men; for it delights in the flesh of men, and above all to it the flesh of men is sweet and welcome food. When it spies some one of men going down to the deepest abyss, those whose toil is the under-sea labour of the brine, then it, light, lifted up above his head, swims unmoved, like the roofs of a hall, unturning, spread about, and goes along, wherever the wretched man goes, and when he stays, settles over him like a lid. As a boy sets a guileful doom for the greedy mice; and the mouse, not divining the ambush of the trap, its belly drives within, and swiftly the hollow vessel above rattles down upon it, and it, for all its eager longing, can no longer escape the strong covering, until the boy seize it and slay it, and laugh over his catch; so that destroying fish spreads itself above the human head, hindering him from rising up, until the breath leaves the man, and he breathes out his soul into the waters; there, when he is dead, the ill-named ox tends him, feasting, having taken by its arts a hard-won prey. And one, marking upon the mossy flats a crab, will praise it and marvel at it for the sake of its gainful craft; for to it too a god gave the prudence to feed on oysters, a sweet and unlaborious meal. The oysters, unfolding the bars of their doors, lick the mud, and craving water are spread open, sitting in their rocky elbows; and the crab, lifting a pebble from beside the breaker, carries it sidelong, gripping with its sharp claws, and draws near in secret, and sets the stone in the midst of the oyster; then, sitting beside it, it feasts on the dear meal; and the oyster, though it strives, has no strength to close its twofold scales, but by constraint is held open, until it dies and sates the hunter. Like to it the crawling sea-stars too contrive; for to them also craft attends upon oysters; but they do not bring a stone as a fellow-worker or helper, those; rather they thrust their rough limb into the midst of the open shells; thus is it pressed, and they feed. The pinna again has its beds in the deep, and in it a fish dwells, called the pinna-guard; she, being feeble, knows neither how to contrive nor how to do anything, but the crab dwells with her in a common home and a common covering, and feeds her and guards her; therefore he is called pinna-guard; but when into the shell a fish comes within, he, scratching her who is unaware with a gainful nip, took the pinna; and she in her pains clapped together her shells, and shut up the prey within for herself and her comrade, and they took a common meal together. So then among the water-faring swimmers also there are some gainful, some senseless, even as among us men, nor is sound thought in all alike. Mark, for senselessness pre-eminent, the day-sleeping fish, which the brine bore most idle of all. Its eyes are turned upward, above its head, and its greedy mouth is in the midst between its eyes; and ever in the sands all day long it lies stretched out sleeping, and by night alone it wakes and roams; therefore it is called the night-creature too; but an evil ruin of an insatiate belly has been its lot; for of food it knows neither surfeit nor any measure, but a boundless, mad-raving voracity it keeps in its shameless belly; nor would it ever cease while food is near, until its very midmost belly bursts apart, and itself, stretched out, falls backward, or some other of the swimmers slays it, laden with its last meal. A sign of its ever-ravening belly I declare to you: for if a man, taking it, should make trial of the chase, offering food with his hand, it will receive it, until right up from its most greedy mouth the food is heaped. Hear, you generations of men, what an end attends greedy follies, what pain follows gluttonies; therefore let one drive joyless idleness far away both from heart and from hand, and keep some measure in food; nor let him take delight of mind in all-feasting tables; for there are many such among men too, for whom the reins are loosed, and they entrust all the cables to the belly; but let a man, looking on, flee the end of the day-sleeper. The sharp-spined sea-urchins too have mind and craft, who know the violence of the winds and the furious storms when they rise, and each heaves up upon its back a stone, as heavy as it may easily carry about its own spines, that against the rush of the wave they may abide, weighed down; for this they dread most, lest the churning surge roll them upon the shores. Of the octopuses I think no one is yet untaught in craft, who make themselves like to the rocks which they embrace and cast their coils about. The hunters of men and the stronger fish alike they easily lead astray by their deceits and escape. But when some weaker creature comes near, straightway the octopuses and the fish appear, leaping out of their rocky shape, and from their guile they both have found food and escaped destruction. In winter, they say, the octopuses never go upon the water of the sea; for they shrink from the furious storms; but they, settling in their hollow chambers, cowering, devour their own feet, as though they were alien flesh; and again, having sated their masters, the feet grow back; this, I suppose, Poseidon has granted them. Such a thought is in the grim, ever-ravening bears too; for shunning the wintry onset of the storm, having dived into the rocky recess of their den, they lick their own paw, an empty work of food, seeking a windy meal, nor will they come forth, until the temperate spring is come to bloom. Above all a hostile hatred have toward one another the darting crawfish and the moray and the octopuses, and they destroy one another with mutual slaughters. Ever among them stands fishy war and battle, and one fills its belly with another. She, setting out from a sea-washed rock, the roving moray darts through the swell of the sea, seeking food, and quickly spies an octopus creeping over the headlands of the shore, and to the welcome hunt she rushes, rejoicing; nor did she escape his notice as she came near; but at first, terrified, he is shaken into fear, nor has any device to escape the moray, crawling as he is, while she swims and is uncontrollably eager. And swiftly she caught him and drove in her blood-red jaw; but the octopus, against his will, fights under deadly constraint, and coils about her limbs, now one way, now another, weaving all manner of twists beneath his crooked thongs, contriving, if by any means he might hold her back, casting his nooses about her; but there is no cure of his ills, no escape; for easily, when he falls about her with his slippery limbs, the nimble moray flows through like water; but he now about her dappled back, now her neck and the tip of her tail casts his coils, and now again falls upon the gates of her mouth and the recesses of her jaws. As when men skilled in limb-strong wrestling long display their strength against one another, and now from their limbs warm and unspeakable sweat pours upon them both; and the nimble gains of their craft wander, and their hands surge about the body; so too the suckers of the octopus, not in order, wandering, labour in vain wrestlings. But she with the sharp-cutting rush of her teeth tears him; and of his limbs some her belly has received, others still in her jaws the swift teeth grind, and others gasp and writhe, half-devoured, still quivering and longing to escape. As when, tracking the trail of serpents through the thickets, the heavy-antlered stag has found by scent the creeping spoor, and comes to the hole and drags the reptile out and devours it eagerly; and it coils about his knees and neck and breast; and the half-eaten joints are scattered, and his teeth carve up many within his mouth; so too the dappled limbs of the ill-fated octopus are tossed; nor did the prudence of his rocky craft save him; for if ever, shunning her, about a rock he twines, and clothes himself in a colour all like to it, yet he escaped not the heart of the moray, but she alone descries him, and the device of that one is fruitless. There you might pity him for his most unseemly doom, how he shrinks among the rocks, while she near him stands as if mocking; so you would say the cruel moray spoke, taunting him: "Why do you cower, crafty one? Whom do you hope to beguile? Soon I will make trial of the rock too, if it will take you within, this crag, and bowing over, hide you." And straightway, fixing her curved fence of teeth, she gorges, tearing him from the crag in his terror; but he in no way, not even as he is rent, leaves the rock nor lets go, but clings to the rock, twined fast, until the very suckers alone are left grown into it. As when, a city being sacked by the hands of foes, the children and the spear-won women being dragged away, a man drags by war's law a boy that has grown fast to the neck and arms of her that bore him, but he, his hands plaited about her, does not let go from her neck, nor does the mother send him forth with wailing, but is herself dragged along with him; so too the cowering body of the dragged octopus clings to the dank crag, and does not let go. The crawfish again devours the moray, harsh though she is exceedingly, subdued by her own self-slaying valour. For he stands near the rock in which dwells the nimble moray; and stretching up his two horns, breathing hostility, he challenges her to come to battle, like the foremost champion of a host, who, trusting in the valour of his hands and his skill in war, having braced his stout body with armour, brandishing his sharp spears, challenges whoever of the foes is willing to meet him; and quickly he rouses another of the champions; so he whets the moray's spirit, nor at the conflict does he linger; and she, darting black from her chamber, arching her neck, raging greatly in her wrath, comes to meet him; but though she presses on him terribly, she harms him not, rough as he is, but in vain just so strikes her jaw against him, and rages fruitlessly with her hard teeth; and they, leaping back from his jaws as from a harsh rock, grow weary and are blunted of their rush. And her wild heart greatly flames and is stirred, until, springing upon her with his long claws, the crawfish grips her by the middle sinew of her neck; and he holds her, fastened on like a bronze pair of tongs, unceasing, nor lets go, though she struggles to escape; and she, labouring with force and vexed with pains, whirls her crooked body every way, and swiftly the sharp-pointed back of the crawfish she casts about, poured around it, and is fixed upon the spikes and sharp points of his shell, and full of close-set wounds she perishes, self-slain, dying by her own folly. As when a man skilled in beast-slaying works, the people gathered in the surrounding theatres, receives upon his long-pointed spear the leopard goaded to fury by the cracking of the whip, standing aslant beneath; and she, even looking on the jaw of the whetted iron, swelling wildly, rears, and into her throat, as into a spear-rack, draws the bronze-wrought point; so too wrath in her folly seized the moray, ill-fated, subdued by self-struck wounds. Such a strife, I suppose, upon the dry land they wage, both in the thickets, the serpent and the rough hedgehog, when they meet; for them too a hostile fate is the care. For the hedgehog, seeing the deadly creeper first, fencing himself with his close-set jutting spines, rolls himself into a ball, guarding his limbs beneath his fence, creeping inward; and the serpent at once darting near him first urges on his venom-bearing jaws, but just so labours an empty toil; for he reaches not within the skin with his fierce teeth, for all his eagerness; such a rugged fleece has beset the other; but the round, rolling ball, whirling his nimble limbs, rolling in close-packed eddies, falls upon the coils and wounds them with the darts of his sharp-cutting hair; and from this side and that flows the bloody ichor, and many wounds afflict him. Then, casting himself about the hedgehog with a coil that runs round on every side, the supple serpent, twined fast in grievous bonds, holds and gnaws and presses on his strength in wrath. But quickly all the spines slip into him, bristling sharp; and he, fixed upon the stakes, neither lets go his force nor against his will is fettered, but stays as if joined by strong bolts, until he dies, and together he has destroyed the serpent too, pressing him often, and to one another they became death and ruin; but often the dread hedgehog has escaped and got away, slipping from the creeper and the dark, inextricable bond, still keeping the spines in the flesh of the dead one. Such a moray too is subdued by evil-minded doom, to the crawfish a welcome and easy meal. The crawfish in turn, both rough and swift though it is, the octopus devours, feebler though it is and sluggish in onset; for when it spies the crawfish beneath the crags, keeping still just so and sitting, then secretly it darts upon his back and casts about its nimble bonds, gripping his strong limbs with its long cords of feet, and with the tips of its suckers it presses the warm tube about the middle of his mouth, squeezing it, nor lets in the breath of air either from within or from the other side; for to the swimmers too the ebbing and flowing air is drawn; so it holds him, fallen upon him; and he swims, now stays still, now gasps, and sometimes against the jutting headlands is dashed; but the other in no way lets go the prize of force, until breath and strength leave him dead. Then, when he has fallen, sitting beside him in the sands, it feasts, as a boy from his nurse's breast draws with his lips again the sweet milk; so it, lapping the flesh, drew it forth out of the keen-edged vessel, sucking, and filled its belly with sweet fare. As a day-sleeping man, with thievish craft plotting unseen evils, never increasing his reverence for justice, at evening, crouching in the narrow streets, has lain in wait for a man passing by from a feast; and the man, heavy with wine, creeps on before, singing a tipsy song, chanting a tune not very sober; but the other in secret rushed up behind and seized his neck with bloody hands, bearing down on him, and laid him in a savage sleep not far from death, and, having stripped him of all his garments, went off, carrying an ill-gotten and hearthless prey; such thoughts have the cunning octopuses too. These are the hostile and unkind ones, pre-eminent among the sea-creatures; and they alone among the dappled fishes are avengers and destroyers of one another. Others among the swimmers are venom-bearing, and in their mouths a foul venom is bred, and a loathsome thing creeps upon their bites. Such too is the centipede-fish, that ill-named reptile of the brine, in body like the reptile of the land; but its hurt is more deadly; for if any draw near and touch it, straightway upon his skin a hot redness inflames, and a weal runs along like that of the grass which they call the nettle, named for the pains. And hateful is the centipede-fish above all to the anglers to come near; for if ever it touch the bait, not one of the swimmers would come near that hook; for such a hateful venom is mingled in it. Such ruin too is bred in the dappled rainbow-wrasses about the mouth; and them most of all the men who search the deeps, the divers and the sponge-cutters, the much-suffering, loathe; for when they spy a searcher of the sea hastening to the bottom in his under-sea labours, they, setting out from the rocks in their myriads, race round the man and pour themselves about him in throngs, and hinder him in his toilsome road, one here, one there, stinging with their shameless mouths; and he grows weary, beset by the water and the hateful rainbow-wrasses, and with his hands, as much strength as is in him, and with hurrying feet drives off the watery host, defending himself; but they pursue unflinching, like the flies that on their works about the harvesting men, toiling in autumn, fly everywhere, the troublesome ranks of summer. And they at once both with toil and with the unmixed strokes of the air sweat, and are vexed by the flies exceedingly; and they relent nothing of their shamelessness, before they die, rather than feed on the tawny blood of the man. Such love have these too, among fishes, for the blood of men. Yet truly no feeble bite has it when it wounds, the creeping octopus or the cuttlefish, but in them too is bred a small but harmful ichor. And piercing stings have they armed themselves with among the fishes, the goby that rejoices in the sands, and the one that rejoices in the rocks, the scorpion-fish, and the swift sea-swallows and the weevers and the dog-fish named for their grievous spines, all sending venom beneath their baneful pricks. But to the sting-ray and the sword-fish a god has placed mighty gifts in their limbs, bracing for each an overpowering weapon; and to the one above its jaw he fixed an upright, self-rooted, pointed thing—not a sword of iron, but a mighty blade strong as adamant. When that lays on its chilling point, not even a very hard stone could endure the wound; such furious and fiery rush is in it. And to the sting-ray there rises from the base of its tail a savage sting, both grievous in force and deadly with venom. Nor would the sword-fish nor the sting-rays first feed in their jaws, before with their blood-red weapons they have wounded whatever is near, living or breathless. But when breath leaves the sword-fish, straightway that strong blade too perishes with it, the weapon is quenched together with its lord, and there is left a useless bone, by no means like to look upon the sword; nor could you, however you wished, do anything with it. But of the sting-ray's wound there is no worse plague, not all the deadly weapons that the hands of smiths have wrought, nor all that on their feathered arrows the Persian poisoners have devised for destruction; for to the sting-ray's life there attends a most chilling shaft, fiery, such as a man shudders to hear of, and it lives when she is dead, and keeps its unwearied, unturning strength; nor does it belch forth deadly ruin on living things alone, whatever it strikes, but a young shoot too and a rock it has marred, if ever it draw near. For if any rich-flourishing plant, growing in its season, with well-formed branches and fruitful offspring, one should wound below, beneath its roots, with that shameless blow, then thereafter, stricken with evil ruin, it ceases from its leaves, and runs down as with a sickness; first it withers from its splendour, nor far off will you see the shoot dry and worthless and bloomless. That weapon once, fitted to a long oar-handled javelin, Circe, the much-drugged mother, gave to Telegonus, to hurl a sea-doom against foes; and he, on the island of the goat-pastures, ran his ship aground, and knew not, sacking the flocks of his own father, but on his venerable sire as he ran to the rescue, on the very man he sought, he wrought an evil doom. There the wily-counselled Odysseus, who had measured countless woes of the sea in his much-laboured contests, the grievous sting-ray slew with a single stroke. And to the tunny and the sword-fish ever attends a companion plague; which they can never turn aside, nor let go nor flee, a savage frenzy seated in their fins, which to them, when the burning Dog-star newly rises, drives in the swift force of its piercing sting, piercing very sharp, and stirs them to grievous madness, arming them with pains; and it urges them, unwilling, to dance with a roving lash; and they with the black wound dart about in madness, now here, now there, they gallop over the wave, holding an unending pain. Often too they have leapt upon the well-horned ships, driven by the ill-tempered rush; often out of the brine they have leapt and run down upon the land, gasping, and exchanged their doom for one of much-laboured pains; for such a dread bite weighs on them and does not let go. For indeed when the hostile gadfly comes near the oxen, and presses its shaft upon their slender flanks, they care nothing for reverence of the herdsmen nor for pasture, but leaving the grass of the herd and all their stalls they rush, sharpened to madness; nor for them does any river, nor the untrodden sea, nor the cleft ravines, nor any unvisited rock check the bull's rush, when the keen-bidding herdsman has roused it to seething, urging it on with hasty pains; everywhere is bellowing, everywhere the leaping of his hoof winds about; such a fierce storm drives him. And this pain is alike for fishes and for oxen. The dolphins greatly lord it over the herds of the sea, exceeding in valour and splendid in beauty, and in swift rush; for like a shaft through the sea they fly; and a flaming gleam most keen they send from their eyes; and even one cowering in the ravines, and one hidden beneath the sands, the fish, they descry. For as among the light birds the kings are the eagles, or among the flesh-eating beasts the lions, as among the creepers the serpents are pre-eminent, so too the dolphins are leaders among fishes. Neither to draw near them as they come, nor to cast the eyes upon them face to face does any fish endure, but they cower far off from the dread leaps of their lord and his snorting breath. And when these rush on, longing for fare, all at once they throw into confusion the unspeakable flocks of the deep, driving them in utter rout; and they fill with fear every path; and the shadowy recesses and the low ravines and the harbours and the sheltered bays of the shores are straitened, as they crowd in from every side; and the dolphin feasts on whichever it will, having chosen the best of the countless that are present. Yet even against these come hostile fishes, those we call the bonitos; nor do they reck of the dolphins, but they alone do battle face to face. Feebler is their body than the tunnies', and about them the flesh is weak, but close-set through their greedy mouth the teeth bristle sharp; therefore they have great courage, nor do they cower before the overpowering leader. For when they spy one rushing off alone, apart from the rest of the dolphins' herd, they, in throngs from this side and that, like a vast host at a summons, gathering into one, set off to the conflict undismayed, as against a tower of foes the warlike shield-bearers charge. The fair-bearded dolphin, against the throng that meets him, at first recks not, but rushes among them, now one, now another snatching greedily as he goes, finding a pleasing feast. But when the ranks of war crown him round on every side, and a great throng circles about him, then indeed the labour sinks already into his heart; and he knew sheer destruction, alone among countless shut in by foes; and the toil of his valour appears. For they, raging in throngs poured about the dolphin's limbs, drive in the force of their teeth; and everywhere they gnaw and cling unyielding, many gripping his head, others his grey chin, others clinging to his very fins, and many have fixed their bloody jaw in his flanks, others seized the tip of his tail, and others below his belly, and others above range over his back, others from his crest, and others hang from his neck. But he, full of toils of every kind, darts through the sea, and within him with frenzy heaves his maddened heart, and his spirit burns with anguish, and everywhere he leaps and writhes, raging without measure, seething with pains; and like a tumbler now through the deep wave he runs like a whirlwind, now is borne to the lowest depth, and often above the brine's foam, leaping up, he springs, in hope the bold swarm of overweening swimmers might let him go; but they, unwearied, let go nothing of their force, but cling to him alike, and as he dives they dive one road with him, and again as he leaps up they dart out of the water with him, dragged along; you would say a new monster was being born to the Earth-shaker, mingled of dolphins and bonitos; so by the grievous gripping of teeth is he fettered. As when a physician, full of devices, draining a wound that is swollen, in which much hostile blood is bred within, the watery broods, the dark-skinned creeping things of the marsh, upon the suffering flesh he sets, to feed on the black blood; and they, at once arched, swell and draw the gore, nor let go, until, having drained again the heavy, undiluted draught of blood from the flesh, they fall off self-rolling, like men drunken; so the bonitos relax not their force before they have carved beneath their mouths that flesh which once they seized. But when they leave him, and the dolphin breathes again from his toil, then you shall see the rage of the leader in his wrath; and a chill ruin appears for the bonitos. For they flee, and he behind, ravaging, like to an ill-sounding waterspout, lays all waste, tearing eagerly, and reddens the sea with blood, striking with his jaws, and, having suffered, avenges the outrage. So too in the thickets, hunters tell, the report goes, the overweening jackals busy themselves about a stag, gathering; for they, darting on with their jaws, snatch away his flesh, and lap the warm spring of the new-shed blood; and he, bleeding with pains, bellowing, full of deadly wounds, now over one mountain top, now another, tosses himself about; and they leave him not, but ever near him follow, the flesh-eaters, and tearing him alive with their teeth they strip off his hide, before death has come upon him, toiling at a most dark and most painful feast. But indeed the shameless jackals paid no penalty, and laughed over the slain stags, while the bold bonitos soon were worsted in a harder strife. This other most pre-eminent deed of the dolphins, hearing of it, I marvelled at: when destructive sickness, the grievous, comes near them, it escapes them not, but they know the end of life; and the sea and the wide depths of the deep fleeing, they run aground upon the light shores; there they breathe out their life and take their lot upon the land, that some one of men may revere the sacred messenger of the Earth-shaker as he lies, and cover him in the heaped sand, remembering his kindly friendship, or that the sea herself, washing him up with the sands, may hide his body, that none of the sea-creatures may behold the leader dead, nor any of the foes do outrage to his body, gone though he is; for valour and might attend even the dying, nor did they shame their glory, even in death. The grey mullet I hear, among all the swimmers of the sea, nurtures the gentlest and most righteous mind; for the grey mullets alone are kindly, and harm neither one of their own tribe nor any of another kind; nor ever do they touch flesh for food beneath their mouths, nor lap blood, but they feed in harmlessness, unstained with blood and harmless, pure broods; they feed either on the green moss of the sea or on the very mud, and lick one another's bodies. Therefore they have a certain honoured reverence among fishes; for none of them harms the young brood, as others do, and they keep off the violence of flesh-eating teeth. So ever among all lie the privileges of reverend Justice, and everywhere she has won a worshipful honour. But all the others go destructive to one another; and therefore you will never see the fishes sleeping, but for them both eyes and mind ever keep wakeful, all-sleepless; since they ever dread the stronger that meets them, and destroy the weaker. The parrot-wrasse alone, they say, the anglers never in the darkness catch falling into their snare, but it sleeps a night-sleep beneath the hollow recesses. Yet it is no marvel that Justice dwells apart from the sea; for of old, the eldest of goddesses, she had not even among mortals her throne, but ill-sounding tumults and rushing Ares, the ruin of men, and Strife, the nurse of much-wept wars, giver of pains, inflamed the wretched race of men of a day; nor were the many distinguished from the beasts at all, but more dreadful than lions, the well-walled towers and the halls and the fragrant temples of the immortals with the blood of men and the sooty smoke of Hephaestus they covered over, until the son of Cronos pitied the ruined race, and to you, the sons of Aeneas, entrusted the earth, kindling it for you. But still, even in the former kings of the Ausonians, Ares raged, arming the Celts and the boastful Iberians, and the long sea-road of Libya and the works of the Rhine, the Ister and the Euphrates; but why should I remember these works of the spear? For now I know you, Justice, nurse of cities, as the hearth-companion and house-mate of men, since for me, set upon the great throne, they rule, both the divine father and the radiant scion; from them a sweet haven of kingship has been spread for me. Them do you protect, and steadfastly guide aright through many decades of the circling years, Zeus and the sons of Heaven, the choir of Zeus, if there is any recompense for piety; and may you bring fulfilling blessedness to the sceptre.

But now come, sceptre-bearer, mark for me the all-cunning devices of the fisher's craft, and the contests of the hunters, and consider the law of the sea, and take delight in our song; for under your sceptre the sea is gathered, and the tribes of Poseidon's channels, and all works among men are furthered for you, and to you the gods released me, a delight and a singer, among the Cilicians beneath the Hermaean shrines.
