And you, Hermes, my father's god, best of the sons of the Aegis-bearer, most gainful mind among the immortals, show forth and signify and begin, guiding the turning-post of my song; for the counsels of the over-subtle fishermen you yourself, lord, first of all devised, and the achievement of the chase of every kind you revealed, weaving dooms upon the fishes. And to Corycian Pan you committed the craft of the deep, your son, who, they say, became the rescuer of Zeus, the rescuer of Zeus, and the destroyer of Typhon. For he, with fisher's baits beguiling the dread Typhon, deceived him to come up out of his cavern, out of the broad pit, and to come to the sea-shore; there the sharp lightnings and the rushes of thunderbolts, blazing, laid him low; and he, burning in the showers of fire, his hundred heads dashed about everywhere among the rocks, torn and rent; and yellow still beside the shores the banks grow red with the gore of the Typhonian shoutings. Hermes, famed in counsel, you above all the fishermen appease; therefore, calling on you along with the rustic gods, I go after the glory of a well-hunting song. First, let the angler have a body and limbs both swift and strong, neither too fat nor too lean of flesh; for there is need often for him to fight against strong fish drawn up, fish with overpowering strength, until in the arms of mother brine they are whirled, struggling, and shaken loose. And there is need to leap from rock and to spring up onto rock easily; and there is need, when the labour of the deep is stretched out, swiftly to thread the long course, and to dive into the deepest places, and, abiding amid the waves, as on the land, to linger, toiling at the works in which upon the sea men contend, holding a steadfast spirit. And let the angler be of a mind cunning and shrewd; since the fish contrive very many and varied things when they fall in with unexpected snares. And let him be most daring and fearless and prudent, nor let him love surfeit of sleep; let him look keenly, wakeful in heart and with open eyes. And let him bear well the storm of Zeus and the thirsty season of Sirius; let him long for toils, and love the sea; for thus he will be both a good hunter and dear to Hermes. The chase by evening in the autumn seasons is strongest, and at dawn when the morning-star rises; in winter set out together with the sun's rays as they are scattered abroad; but the whole day in flowering spring is enriched with hunts of every kind, when all the fishes, haunting the shores near the land, are drawn on by the labour of birth and the thirst of love. And ever look toward the wind that blows gentle and fair, rolling the soft brine lightly; for violent winds the fishes dread and hate, nor do they wish to wheel about over the sea; but in a temperate wind the chase stands favourable on every hand. And all the swimmers of the sea dart against the winds and the waves, since for them the road is thus easier as they go toward the shores, nor by constraint do they labour, driven from behind by the gusts. But let the fisher set forth, spreading his net to the breezes fair: toward the North, when the wet South wind blows; and toward the Southern sea, when the North wind drives; and when the East wind rises, toward the paths of the West; and against the East let the West wind bear his boat; for thus the swarms unspeakable will meet him, and good shall be the catch. In four ways have the fishers contrived the law of sea-hunting; and some take delight in hooks, and of these some, fastening to long reeds the well-twisted line of horse-hair, hunt; and others, just so binding from their hands a flaxen cord, send it forth; and one delights in lines let straight down, and another glories in many-hooked lines. Nets again others care more to make ready; of these some are casting-nets, and some are called draw-nets, and trawls and round hand-nets and seines; and others they call covering-nets, and along with seines, the foot-ropes and the cork-floats together and the crooked all-catcher; and countless and varied are such nets of the snare-stitching folds. And others again set their mind rather on weels, weels, which have cheered their masters as they slumbered at their ease; for from small toil a great gain attends. And others wound the swimmers with the long-barbed trident from the land and from the ship, as they wish. And the measure of all these, and the order of each, they know exactly, those who fashion these things. For the fishes had not only against one another a close device and thievish craft, but they have even often deceived the prudent hunters themselves, and fled the violence of the hooks and the bellies of the all-catchers, when already caught, and outran the wits of men, conquering by counsel, and became a grief to the fishermen. The grey mullet, drawn in the plaited arms of the net, was not ignorant of the encircling snare, but springs up high, longing for the top of the water, straight upward, hastening with what strength he has, in a light leap to rush; nor did he fail of his prudent counsel; for often by his springs he has leapt over even the topmost cork-ropes easily, and escaped his doom. But if, having sprung up at the first attempt, he slips again into the noose, then he no longer forces his way nor leaps up, grieving, but, taught by trial, ceases from his rush. As when a man, long tossing in a sickness full of cares, at first, both longing and clinging to life, obeys the physicians in all things, whatever they bid, doing them; but when the inescapable dooms prevail, the dooms of Hades, then he cares no more for life, but stretched out he lies, having yielded to death his fainting limbs, already looking on his last day near his fate; so too the grey mullet learns what end is coming, and lies fallen, awaiting the doom of the hunter. And the morays, when at any time they fall into the nets, seeking a wide gap, wheel about in the toils, and darting through it after the manner of serpents, all with their slippery limbs slip out and escape. And the bass, having dug a pit with his fins through the sand, as large as to receive his body, reclines as into a bed; and when the fishermen draw their net to the shores, he, lying just so in the mud, gladly escaped and fled the snare of destruction. Such things the mormyrus too contrives: when it perceives the chase coming on, falling forward, it dives into the sands. But the bass, struck by the point of the well-curved hook, springing up high, presses its head unceasingly against the very line, forced, that its wound may become wider, and that it may escape destruction. Such things the great-bulked orcyni too devised; for when they have snatched the jaw of the bent guile, swiftly straining they dart down to the lowest deep, forcing the hand of the hunter; and if they reach the bottom, then straightway, striking their head against the ground, they break open the wound, and spit out the barb. But when the monstrous fish gape at the lines let down—such as are the broods of oxen and of sheep, or the ray, or the sluggish race of the hake—they will not follow, but casting their broad body upon the sands they all together weigh down, and lay toil upon the fishers; and often they slipped off, loosed from the hook. And the nimble bonitos and the thresher-sharks, when they are caught, straightway hasten upward to anticipate, and quickly the middle of the line they cut beneath their teeth, or the very tips of the hair; therefore for them the fishers have forged a longer shank upon the hook, a defence against their teeth. Yes, and the cramp-fish does not abandon its own wit even when distressed by the blow; but strained with pains it presses its flanks against the line; and swiftly through the hair of horse and through the reed it ran and into the fisher's right hand it hurled the fish-named pain; and often from his hand the rod fell, and the gear of the chase. For such a frost settles at once upon the hand. The cuttlefish again has such guileful devices. There is in them, fixed in their poppy-pouches, a dark ink, darker than pitch, an unseen drug of watery gloom, which is bred in them as a defence against destruction; and them, when fear takes them, straightway they belch up the murky drops, and all about the sea, the dim ichor stains and blots out all the paths around, and turns aside all sight; and they, through the murky passage, at once flee easily both man and, if anywhere, a stronger fish. Like to them contrive the air-roaming broods of the squid; but in them the ink is not black but ruddy that is bred, and a device all like to theirs they make ready. With such thoughts they are minded; but nonetheless they perish by the close prudence of the fishermen. Those that run in the towering open seas they easily draw up; for in them is no varied wit; for already one has drawn up even with onions and bare hooks the open-sea-roaming fish. But all that feed near the sea-fenced land, for them the mind is sharper; but even of these the small are drawn up with feebler shrimps, gaping at the fringes of octopuses or at a crab and at small hermit-crabs, and if you should fix salt flesh and rock-worms, and whatever fishy thing is near you; and arm the small as bait for the greater; for laughing at their meals they hasten on destruction; for ever foolish is the race of the swimmers that run. The corvina lures the tunny, and the bass the shrimp, the fat one, and the channus is a dear bait for the braize, and the bogues for the dentex, and the rainbow-wrasses for the dolphin-fish; the red mullet slays the orphos, and the perch draws up the cirrhis, and the gilthead is drawn up with the sprat; while the loathsome morays are borne, hastening after the flesh of octopuses; and all that have a body exceeding in size— the beauty-fish is gladdened with the tunny, while with the hake the orcynus, and the bass you should arm against the anthias, the dolphin-fish with the sword-fish, and on the glaucus you should fix the grey mullet; and for one fish a different kind you should devise, for the stronger the weaker; since indeed all of them are to one another both dear food and greedy destruction. So there is nothing worse than hunger nor than the heavy belly, which rules among men, harsh and a grievous mistress, a hearth-companion, never forgetting its dues, and many, swerving from their wits, it casts into ruin and binds fast in shames; and the belly rules over the beasts and the creeping things and the flocks of the air, and most of all among the swimmers it holds power; for to them the belly is ever doom. First learn the prudent hunting of the anthiae, such as the dwellers of our glorious fatherland make ready, above the Sarpedonian shore, all that dwell in the city of Hermes, the ship-famed town of Corycus, and in sea-girt Eleusa. Those rocks near the land the skilled man marks out, beneath which the anthiae make their lodging, cavern-grown, with their close clefts riven through; and sailing up in his boat, he makes a loud-ringing din, beating with planks; and the heart of the anthiae delights in the clatter; and one comes up at once from the deep, peering at boat and man; and to him the angler straightway throws ready perch in the waves, or corvinae, offering the gifts of a first stranger's fare. And he, greedily rejoicing, feasts on the dear meal, and fawns upon the crafty hunter. As when into the dwelling of a hospitable man there comes a renowned man, in works either of hand or of mind, and he gladly saw him at his hearth, and with gifts well and with feasts and kindnesses of every sort cherishes him; and both, rejoicing about the table, take delight in the alternate cups of the mixing-bowl; so the angler, rejoicing in his hopes, smiles, and the fish takes delight in the new meals. Thence thereafter he, day by day, ever to the rock sets out, nor leaves off his labour nor abandons it, bringing the feast; and they at once gather in throngs, the feasters, throughout the place, as at a summoner's bidding. And ever to more and to readier he offers the greedy fare; nor have they other roads nor other recesses in their minds, but staying there they linger, as in the folds of herdsmen the flocks lodge in the wintry days, nor at all longing to go forth from the pen. And when they descry, rising from the land and hastening with oars, the nurturing boat, at once all upright, exulting, wheeling above the brine, they play delightfully and come to meet their nurse. As when to her unfledged nestlings a mother bears food, the bird that is the first herald of the spring west wind, and they, softly twittering, leap up in the nest, joyful about their mother, and longing for food open wide their beaks, and all the house resounds of the host-receiving man, shrilly crying to its young; so they, when their feeder comes to meet them, joyful leap up, as in a dancer's ring. And the fisher, fattening them with meals one upon another, touching them with his hand and stretching gifts from his hand, gentles their dear heart; and at once, as to a king, they obey him, and wherever he beckons with his hand they swiftly dart; and he now behind the ship, now in front, now near the mainland sends his right hand; and you will see them, like boys by a man's prudent care in a wrestling-ground, darting this way and that, where the overseer bids. But when of tending he has enough, and the chase is his care, then indeed, fastening the line about his left hand he sits, and the barb of the hook, strong and swift, he makes ready, and them he turns aside, bidding with his hand all alike, or, taking a stone, he cast it through the water; and they dive after it, thinking it to be food; and of them one only he left out, chosen, whichever he will, the ill-fated one, rejoicing in his last meals; the hook he held out above the brine; and he the ruin swiftly snatched, and the eager man drew with both hands, having taken a quick and thievish catch; and he escapes the notice of the other troop of anthiae; for if they should see or hear the splash of the ill-caught one drawn up, no more will there be for him so many meals, that they should come back again, but they spit it out, loathing both the tending and the deadly place; but let one be strong, and forcefully overpowering let him draw it up, or let a second other lay hold of the labour; for thus, not perceiving their own crafty ruin, they themselves, being fattened, fatten their fellows; and ever, when you will, a well-aimed catch shall be at hand. Others, trusting in strong force and in the might of their limbs, arm themselves for a great contest against the anthias, toiling at no friendship, no food, but to the point of the hook they hasten, and overcome by valour. The hook is made of hard bronze or of iron, and twofold barbs hold on each side a great flaxen cord; and about it they drive a living bass, if it is at hand; but if it die, quickly someone puts beneath its mouth a leaden weight, which they call the dolphin; and it, with the heavy lead, bends and bends back its head, like a living thing. And the cord is strong and well-plaited; but when the din the anthiae hear and leap up out of the sea, to others belongs the labour of the oar, but he, from the very stern, the fisher sends the curved guile into the sea, softly whirling it round; and they at once all follow the ship and the fleeing thing, beholding it like a fish, hastening after the feast, and dart forth each before the other; you would say that against a hostile man a man was lightening his knees in terror; and they long for noble victory; and whichever the angler sees to be pre-eminent, to that one he offered the feast; and it greedily gaping at the gifts—ill gifts—pursued; thence thereafter you shall behold the strength of both, what a contest they wage, the man and the fish drawn along; for his stout arms and his brow and his shoulders and the sinews of his neck and his ankles surge with strength and are strained with valour; while the fish, vexed beneath its pain, struggles, dragging him who drags it, forcing to dive into the sea, uncontrollably eager; and he calls on his comrades to fall to the oars; and as the boat is driven on, backward from the stern the whole is dragged by the fish's rush; and the line cries out, and from his hand blood drips as it is sawn; but he in no way lets go the heavy struggle. As when two overweening men, eager in strength, straining ropes upon one another, strive to drag, pulling with backward heaves, and long both, bearing equal measures of toil, unceasingly draw and unceasingly are drawn; so for these, the fisher and the fish, has strife arisen, the one longing to dart away, the other to drag. Nor do the other fish leave it in its pains, the anthiae, but they wish to defend it, and against the man himself they thrust their backs by force and each one falls upon him, foolish, nor perceived that they were wearing out their own comrade. And often, longing with their jaws to break the cord, they are helpless, since their mouth is weaponless. And late, as it labours in toil and pains, the man, forcing it with close strokes of the oars, drew it up; but if it yield to him even a little, then no more will he draw it; for such an overweening strength has it. And often, over its sharp-pronged spine, biting it through, it cut the line, and darted away, leaving the hunter empty. Such strength has the beauty-fish too, and the breed of the orcyni, and all the others that, monstrous of body, roam; with such arms they are hunted. Others again, beguiling with meals and feasts, the fisher hunts; and a good fish for him will be the cantharus, which ever delights in the scaly rocks. And you should plait a round weel, the largest you can, making it either of Iberian broom or of withies, casting the rods about; and let its entrance be smooth and its belly wide-gaping; and within you should set as bait a creeping octopus or a crawfish, both roasted from the fire; for the savour draws the fishes within. Thus, having made ready the woven guile near the rock, you should lean it aslant, an under-sea ambush; and at once the smell will rouse the cantharus and it will come within the weel, not very bold on its first road, but most swiftly having feasted, it runs back again; thence thereafter the weel-man for those ever puts in fresh delightful fare; and them quickly the ill-named belly gathers within, and one brings another as a fellow-supper comrade. And now, fearless, in throngs within the weel gathered, sitting all day long, as though a house they had won, they abide, and have found an evil lodging. As when, in the house of an orphaned youth, others of his age, caring nothing for prudence, both bidden and self-invited all day long gather, ever consuming the substance of the unguarded house, such as reckless youth lets loose upon foolish young men, and in their folly they have found an evil end; so for these gathered there ruin stands close at hand. For when they are many and well-fattened, then the man covers the mouth of the weel with a lid well-fitted; and them, crouched within the toil, slumbering for the last time, he drew up; and late, perceiving destruction, they gasp and are eager to slip out, the fools, nor any more have the weel so well-housed. For the admones they arm an autumn weel of osier, and moor it amid the waves, fastening below a pierced stone as anchor; and corks hold the guile above; and within it ever they cast four wet pebbles from the shore; and on these, as they are wetted, there grows a milky sea-slime, the longing for which draws the fishes, small, worthless, a greedy race; and they gather, running on to the weel, and stay within its arms. And the admones, seeing within the hollow recess the gathered ones, soon all rush upon them, desiring the feast; but them they reach not, but slip past easily; and they, for all their longing, are not able again to slip out of the woven ambush, but, contriving woes for others, they have found destruction for themselves. As when in the thickets a mountain rustic sets a trap for a beast, and in his pitiless heart within binds it tight, cutting off a dog's loins; and from its pains, a ringing din of the suffering creature comes from afar, and around it the thicket groans; and the leopard, hearing, was gladdened and rushes on, seeking the track of the cry; and quickly it came and leapt in; and then him the hidden guile snatches up on high, while she in the pit is rolled, fallen forward, and cares no more for the feast, but for fear; and for her there is no ready way out; such things the wretched admones too suffered, and instead of food they rushed upon doom and the inescapable fence of Hades. And one too, for the shads alike and the chalcides, has devised an autumn chase, and took the larinus and the tribes of the horse-mackerel, weaving a weel of broom well-compacted, and put in a cake of roasted vetch, soaked in fragrant wine, and mixed in the tears of the Assyrian maiden, Theias' daughter, who once, they say, having loved her father, accomplished a hopeless deed and came to that union, Aphrodite being wroth; but when fate of the gods rooted her into a tree of her name, she wails and laments her ruin, wet with tears for the grace of the bed; and mixing in her divine sap, he moors the weel in the breakers, and at once a lily-fragrance ran over the sea, calling the manifold herds; and they follow, shaken by the delicious breath, and swiftly the weel is filled, bringing the hunter a good return of the chase. The saupes ever in the wet seaweeds most of all delight, and with that food are they hunted. In the former days the angler sails to one place, and ever amid the waves he casts pebble-stones, having tied about them flourishing weeds. But when the fifth dawn looks on the labour, and the saupes, gathered, feed about that passage, then he makes ready the guile of the weel; and within it he cast stones wrapped in weeds, and about the mouths he bound sea-grasses, in which they delight, the saupes and all other plant-eating fish; they then, gathering, ate the grasses, but afterward were swept into the recess; and he at once draws up the weel, swiftly sailing back; and in silence is his work accomplished, with voiceless men and with noiseless oars; for silence is profitable for all hunts, but above all among the saupes; since for them the mind is easily startled; and startling makes the labour hard to hunt. Of the red mullet none, I say, in baser foods delights; for all the refuse of the sea, whatever it meets, it feeds on; and it longs above all for an ill-savouring feast; and exceedingly it delights in human bodies that are rotting, when the mournful sea has taken some one. Therefore with baits that breathe out a stench easily they draw it, all that breathe a hostile reek. And like, I say, to the red mullets and to swine are their habits made, ever wallowing about the belly's urge; and both—the mullets are distinguished among the swimmers, and the swine are pre-eminent among the herds of the land. But you shall not carry off the melanurus, neither in a weel easily beguiling it, nor in the flaxen circle; for above all the melanurus among fishes is both feeble and prudent, and never is greedy food welcome to its heart; and ever, when there is calm, it lies in the sands, and does not come up from the brine; but when the surging sea presses hard about, from violent winds, then indeed the melanuri alone dart through the wave in throngs, dreading neither any man nor any sea-creature; while all the rest in fear dive to the lowest foundation of the sea, they then haunt the loud-resounding shores and draw near the rocks, wanderers, if any food the sea, beaten by the gusts, should show forth; the fools, nor did they learn how much wiser are men, who took them in the chase even when they utterly shunned it. When the wintry flood of Amphitrite seethes, a man stands upon a jutting sea-beaten rock, where the keenest wave roars about the crags; and he scatters food upon the breaking surges, cheese mingled together with Demeter's grain; and to the welcome fare the melanuri leap, hastening on. But when they are at hand in throngs for the cast of the chase, he turns his body aslant, that the water may not be shadowed by his craft and fear be in the fishes; and there is for him a slender reed ready in his hands, and a slender line of light hair, unplaited just so; and with slender hooks, close-set, it is plaited; on these he put the bait, which before too he had cast through the water, and sends it into the deep churning wave; and they, seeing it, at once leap up and snatch their destruction. Nor has the fisher an idle hand, but often he draws up the hooks from the eddy, even if often they be empty; for of the surging sea he could not perceive exactly, whether any fish is caught, or whether just so the waves toss them about; but when one gapes upon it, swiftly he drew it out before laying the guile in his mind, before fear smites the worthless melanuri. Such a wintry, all-thievish chase he accomplished. Yes, and the grey mullet too, though it is not greedy, they beguiled, having set upon the narrow hooks food mingled with Demeter's grain and with the curdled gifts of milk; and they kneaded into them together fragrant mint, which once they say was a maiden, a being of the underworld, the Cocytian Nymph; and she inclined to the bed of Aïdoneus; but when the maiden Persephone he ravished from the Aetnaean crag, then her, crying out with overweening words, raging insolently in jealousy, in wrath Demeter ground to dust, trampling on her with her sandals; for she had said that she was more glorious in form and better in beauty than dark-eyed Persephone, and that to herself Aïdoneus would return, and her from his halls would drive out; such ruin leapt upon her tongue. And a worthless herb, named for her, sprang from the earth, which kneading in they cast upon the hooks. And the grey mullet, not long after, when the smell reached it, meeting it, at first from afar off the hook askance beneath its eyes beholds the guile, like a man, a stranger, who, coming upon much-trodden crossroads, stands pondering, and his heart now to the left, now to the right is minded to go upon the path; and he peers on either side, and his mind like a wave rolls, and very late he reached for a single counsel; so too in the grey mullet his spirit ponders all manner of things, suspecting both the guile and harmless food; and late his mind roused him and led him near his fate; and at once, trembling, he drew back; and often already fear seized him as he touched, and turned back his rush. As when a little girl child, her mother being away, longing for a dainty or some other thing, trembles to touch it for fear of her mother's wrath, nor to draw back, for all her longing, has she the heart; but creeping up in secret she turns away again, and her heart now has courage, now dread fear falls upon it; and her eyes ever peer keenly, strained toward the doorway; so then, drawing on, the gentle fish wheels back. But when, taking courage, it comes near, not very readily does it touch the food, but with its tail first it lashes, rousing the hook, lest perhaps some warmth of breath be in the flesh; for to grey mullets it is forsworn to feed on what is living. Thence thereafter with the tips of its mouth it nibbles, scraping the feast round; and the fisher at once with the bronze pierces it, jerking it up, as a man checking a bold horse, a charioteer with the hard constraints of the bit, drew it up, and cast it gasping upon the hateful land. And the sword-fish too they beguiled with deadly hooks. But not for the sword-fish is such a doom, nor like the others'; for not upon hooks do they set ready the food, but it is hung bare and unconcealed, the cord being barbed at its end with double points; and of that, hanging above about three palms, a soft white fish, one, by the tip of its lip they bound skilfully; and when the furious sword-fish comes, straightway it carves the fish's body with its greedy blade; and as it is being cut up, the joints of the bound thing fall away, and it whirls about the very jaws of the hook; but it knew not the bent guile, but gaping at the heavy feast, the prey is drawn up by the man's strength. And many against the sword-fish the hunters arm, above all those who hunt the Tyrrhenian sea-passage and about Massalia, the holy city, and about the Celts; for there both dread and like to no fishes, unapproachable, the great-bulked sword-fish range. And they, fashioning boats likened to the sword-fish themselves, both a fishy body and swords, guide them against it; and it does not shun the chase, thinking it not well-benched ships that it beholds, but other sword-fish, a common race, until the men on every side encircle it; and it perceived its ruin too late, pierced by the three-pronged point, nor has it strength to flee, for all its longing, but by constraint must be subdued. And often, in defence, it has pierced the hollow side of a ship clean through with its sword, the valiant fish, but they, swiftly, with strokes of the well-bronzed axe have broken off all the sword from its jaws; and so in the ship's wound the spike sticks fast, and it is drawn up bereft of its strength. As when, contriving a war-guile against foes, longing to come within the towers and the city, having stripped the armour from the war-slain dead, they themselves armed and ran near the gates; and the others, thinking it their own hastening citizens, open the doors, and rejoiced not in such comrades; so too the likeness of ships beguiled the sword-fish. And indeed, in the crooked arms of the net encircled, the sword-fish, greatly foolish in its follies, perishes, which leaps, eager to slip out, but trembling near the woven guile, again backward it withdraws; nor has it weapon in mind, such as is fixed in its jaws, but cowardly it stays with fainting spirit, until they draw it out upon the shores; and there with timbers, the men driving down with strokes one upon another, crushed its head together, and it perishes by a foolish doom. Folly took the mackerel too, and the fat tunny, and the needle-fish and the tribes of the far-scattered dentex. The mackerel, seeing others crouched within the snare, longed to enter the net's many-meshed destruction; such a delight comes upon them as they look on; like to untried children, who, beholding the bright flashing of kindled fire, warmed by its rays laugh, and long to touch it and stretch their childish hand into the flame; but soon the cruel fire was revealed to them; so they long to fall into the inescapable ambush, into its recess, and met with an evil love. There some, running aground in the wider meshes, leapt out, while others, shut in the narrow passages, endured a bitter, constricted doom, accomplishing it. And many, as the net is drawn to the shores, you shall see fastened on both sides as with bolts, some still minded to enter the snare of destruction, others already eager to slip out of their misery, held within by the wet meshes. The tunnies again toil the same toil as the mackerel in folly; for to them too a like longing for ruin falls, to mingle in the flanks of the guileful net; but for them there is no diving down into the belly within, but they dart at it with their crooked teeth, plotting with their body a sufficient passage; and in their teeth, as they press the wet net, it is stretched; nor any device to escape, but, labouring in the bond about their mouths, they are drawn to the land, taken by their follies. And indeed such is the wit of the needle-fish: when they have fled out of the bosom of the net, and got outside the toil, again they turn about, and, wroth at the net, they drive in their bites; and it sinks within them and holds fast their close teeth within. But the dentex go in equal companies, distinguished; and to them, when a man lets down a hook, they all, turning away, an askance light upon one another cast, and will not draw near; but when one, darting out of another row, swiftly the bait snatches, then another too takes courage in his heart and draws near the hook and is dragged; and they, beholding one another, rejoicing about the feast, are gladdened as they are dragged, and hasten, each before the other, who shall die first being caught, like children exulting in their toys. The race of the tunnies is sprung from the wide-pathed Ocean; and they come to the works of our sea in spring, after the frenzy, when they rage with the madness of mating. And these first, within the Iberian brine, the men hunt who glory in their strength, the Iberians; secondly, by the mouth of the Rhone, the hunters, the Celts and the ancient dwellers of Phocaea; thirdly they hunt, all who in the Trinacrian isle are dwellers and by the waves of the Tyrrhenian sea. Thence in the boundless depths, one here, another there, they scatter and sail over all the sea. Great and dread is the chase that comes to the fishermen, when the spring host of the tunnies sets out. First of all they mark out a place of the sea neither too narrow under the overhanging banks nor too open to the winds, but bearing measures fitting both of clear sky and of sheltering recesses. There first onto a steep, high hill the skilled tunny-watcher climbs, who marks the manifold herds as they come, both of what kind and how many, and declares it to his comrades; and at once all the nets like a city are set forward in the waves; and there are gate-keepers to the net, and gates, and inmost galleries. And they swiftly rush on in rows, like phalanxes of men coming on rank by rank; some are younger, some older, others in the midst of their prime; and countless they flow within the nets, until they are willing, and the net takes up the gathered ones; and rich and pre-eminent stands the catch.

Others, as prey for hunters, watery desire led on; with deadly couplings, with deadly love they met, hastening to their amorous ruin. But you, O mightiest of city-guarding kings, yourself, Antoninus, and the godlike heart of your son, listen with favour and take joy in the delights of the sea, such as the gently-giving Muses have decked my mind with, and have crowned with the gift of inspired song; and grant me to mingle for your ears and your minds a sweet, clear stream.

Cruel Love, deviser of wiles, of the gods most fair to look upon, but most grievous when you stir the heart, falling unforeseen, and like a storm beneath the breast you mingle, breathing the sharp menace of fire, seething with pains and with unmixed sorrows; to shed the warm grace of the tear, and to hear from the depths the groan, and beneath the inward parts to redden with a hot flush, and to strip from the skin its bloom, turned awry, and to hollow the eyes, and to lift the whole mind beside them to madness; many you have rolled into death, all those you met as a wintry and savage foe, bringing frenzy; for in such feasts you delight. Whether among the blessed you are oldest in birth, risen out of unsmiling Chaos, ablaze with sharp fire, and were the first to yoke the ordinances of marriage, the first to set a bound upon the bridal furrows; or whether Aphrodite of Paphos, ruler and wise, bore you, a winged god lifted upon wings, be gracious, and come to us mild and serene, keeping measure; for none refuses the work of Love. Everywhere you rule, and everywhere they long for you and greatly tremble; happy is he who tends a temperate love and guards it in his breast. For you, neither the heavenly race suffices nor the human stock: you spurn not even the beasts, nor all that the barren air feeds; you plunge beneath the depths of the lowest pool, and you arm black shafts even among the fish, that nothing of your power be left untaught, not even the fish that swims below the wave.

What love for one another, what sharp-pointed longing the dappled parrot-wrasses keep, nor in their troubles do they forsake each other, but with defending heart often, when one is struck by the bloody hook, another parrot-wrasse, darting up as champion, shears the line with its teeth and saves its comrade, and blunts the snare and grieves the angler. And one already caught within the back-woven creels another steals away and drags out of destruction: for when the gleaming fish falls into the creel's ambush, at once it perceives, and to escape the evil it strives, and turning down its head and eyes, backward toward its tail it swims up, crossing the barrier; for it fears the long-pointed rushes that bristle all round the gateway and wound the eyes of one coming against them, like sentinels. But the others, seeing it whirling helplessly, come from outside to its aid, nor do they leave the tormented one; and one, holding out its tail like a hand, gives it for the comrade within to seize; the other grips with its teeth, and he drags it forth from death, its guiding tail held as a bond beneath the mouth. And often, when the captive within holds out its tail, another seizes it and drags it forth, following it; by such devices they escape their doom. As when men climb a rugged hill through the gloom of shadowy night, when the moon is hidden and the cloud-veils grow black, and they struggle in the dark and wander on untrodden paths, holding each other by the hand, drawn and drawing, a relief from their toils in turn; so do these by mutual love become defenders of one another; yet this devised destruction for the wretches, and they met a deadly and painful love, undone by the cunning of the fishers. Four hunters embark in the swift boat, of whom two attend to the labour of the oars, the third weaves a crafty design. Tying a female parrot-wrasse, he trails it by the very tip of its lip in the eddies, bound to a line of flax; it is best to draw it up alive; but if it die, after its mouth he takes the dolphin-trick of lead. And from the cord at the other end behind is driven a heavy rounded cube of lead at the knot's end; and so, like one alive among the waves, the female is trailed and stretched out by the fisher. The fourth draws the creel's deep snare against them from close by; and the others, seeing it, rush straight on, swiftly hastening, the dappled parrot-wrasses, to rescue the one drawn along, and they course round the deceit on every side, driven by frenzied desire for the female; and with their oars the men speed the boat with all their might; and the fish follow eagerly; soon their aid proves their very last. For when the angler's mind sees them gathered and raging unrestrained toward frenzy for the female, he set in the creel together the net and the lead, which, weighing down the parrot-wrasse, drew it within; and they at once, as soon as they saw, poured in to outstrip one another, urging on the woven fence of Death, and in their eager throng the bars of withy and the dread gape of the gateway are crowded; for such gadflies drive them on. As when men devoted to the contests of swift feet, launched from the starting-line at full speed, stretching their nimble limbs forward, strain to accomplish the long course; and in all is the desire to reach the post and to win the sweet-giving prize of victory and to dart toward the door and to gird on the strength of triumph; so great a love leads even these on to leap into the chambers of Hades, the ambush from which none returns. With most dog-like and final frenzy for love, self-surrendered, they fill the men with a longed-for catch.

Others again set the living female within the dark creel and place it beneath those rocks where the milk-white parrot-wrasse haunts; and they, by love's breath bewitched, gather round in amorous longing, and lick about it and search on every side, seeking the way down into the creel; and at once they reach the wide entrance, which holds a barrier with no way out, and all fall in together in a crowd, nor is there any means to escape, but they found a hateful end to their loves. As one who plots a guileful death for birds hides in the leafy thickets a female bird, the familiar comrade of the same-tongued hunt; and she shrills out her clear-toned song, and they, hearing it, all press on, and rush themselves into the noose, led astray by the cries of the female's voice; so did those fall into the flanks of the creel, like them.

Cuttlefish too, ill-fated in love, run on to greater ruin; for against them the fishers, mournful of the sea, send neither the deadly creel nor the casting-folds of the net, but they simply trail one alone, fastened, among the waves; and the others, when from afar they see it, at once come against it, and twined about it cling fast, grown into its coils, as when girls from a foreign land have seen a long-absent brother, or a kindly father come home unharmed to the halls; or as a girl, newly taken under the yoke of wedded Aphrodite, captured in the well-caught bond of marriage, twines about the bridegroom, all night long looping fetters about his neck on either side with her white arms; so then do the cunning cuttlefish twist about one another; nor is the work of love let go until the fishers drag them up to the boat; and still they are grown together, and with their love at once they took their doom. These too men beguile with creels in the season of spring; for shading the creels with sprigs of tamarisk or with the budding leaves of the arbutus, or with other foliage, they set them on the much-sanded shores; and these, needing both offspring and a bed, hasten into the creel, and sitting among the leaves there they ceased their longing, and ceased too their wretched life, drawn up by the cunning fishers.

Beyond all the fish a grievous love the merle endures, and his heart blazes for the wrasses, raging with frenzy and jealousy, a heavy-minded daemon. For the merle there is no single mate sharing his haunt, no single wife, no single chamber, but many wives, and many separate clefts hide the home-set beds of his women; in these always, all day long, within the hollow recesses the wrasses dwell, like newly-wedded brides, whom none would see going forth before the chamber; in them burns the modesty of marriage; so these, each shut within the chambers, always linger where their husband himself bids. The merle in turn, sitting by the rocks, never leaves, always keeping watch over his beds, nor ever turns to another, but all day long he wheels about, and now to these, now to those chambers he peers, and his mind is set neither on food nor has any other care, but over his brides he toils, jealous, with ever-watchful labours; by night he thinks of food and rests from his works just so much as breaks his unceasing guard. But when the wrasses are in the throes of bearing their young, then he darts about, beyond restraint, trembling all round them, and goes now to this, now to that wife, much like one trembling in travail. As a mother frets in her heart, shuddering at the swift birth-pangs of her cherished daughter in her first labour, for that is the great fear of women; and to herself comes no lesser wave of Eileithyia's pains, and on all sides she is shaken through the chambers, praying, groaning, with her heart in suspense, until from within she hears the cry that ends the pain; so he, trembling for his brides, his heart greatly blazes. Some such law of marriage, I hear, the Assyrians follow, who hold their towns beyond the ford of Tigris, and the dwellers in Bactra, the far-shooting nation of arrows; for among these too many women hold the marriage-beds, set apart, and all sleep with the man in turn, changing nights; and after them follows the sting of grievous jealousy, and over jealousy they are destroyed, always whetting a heavy war against one another. So no grief worse than jealousy is bred in men, and it makes many laments and many wailings; for it is the comrade of shameless frenzy; and gladly it consorts with frenzy, and into heavy ruin it dances out, and its end is destruction. This too led the wretched merle into ruin to be overcome, and he met a harsh recompense for his loves. For when the angler sees him circling on the rocks, a fish troubled over his brides, he fixes upon his strong hook as quickly as may be a living prawn, and above the hook a heavy cube of lead is hung; and stealthily he lets the heavy snare down toward the rocks, and close by their chambers he whirls it; and the fish, seeing it, at once stirred up rushed forth, hoping the prawn was coming into his home, hostile to his beds and to his brides; and rushing on at once he hopes within his jaws to punish the prawn's coming, nor did he perceive his own doom, gaping wide upon it; but the fisher, marking him at once, pierced him through, jerking up with his bronze jaws, and drew him forth, struggling and gasping his last, and somewhere taunted him with such mocking words: Now indeed, now keep watch and guard your brides, poor wretch, and staying in your chambers take joy in your brides; for not one Cypris pleased you, nor one bed, but greatly you exulted, sole husband in so many beds; yet come here now, your marriage is ready, bridegroom, the gleam of the white-crowned fire on land. Such taunts he flung, telling them to one who could not hear. And the wrasses, when their guardian husband dies, going abroad wander from the chambers, and shared with the man a common doom.

And indeed by love and by mutual aid the dog-fishes perish, and the tribes of the dark horn-bearing rays; the white fish is caught fast upon the hook, and the angler, going where the dim mud sits deep below in the long fathoms, let down the hook, and swiftly one met it and seized the bait; he is hauled up at once, and the others marking it, all in a throng follow close, that they may come to the very boat and the hunters. Then you might take some in the round circle of the landing-net, and others, striking down with the iron three-pronged spears, and with various snares; for they do not turn aside and flee until they see their comrade hauled up, and they wish to perish together. As when from the hall the corpse of a son newly slain, their cherished one, his parents bear to the much-wept tomb, for whom they will toil long in vain; torn with grief, wailing over their child, they cling to the mound and will not return to their home, but are eager to die with the dead in shared mourning; so these will not be left behind when their fellow is hauled up, until they too are destroyed by the hunters.

Others a strange love, not native to the brine, seized, rousing in fish a land-born madness beyond the sea; what a shaft of alien affection comes upon the octopus and the sargue-kind, comrades of the rocks. The octopuses love the shoots of Athena and the grey branches, and they draw a longing for them; a great marvel indeed, to be drawn in heart toward a tree and to rejoice in the sprigs of the sleek plant. For where, near the sea, stands the bright-fruited olive, flourishing on the neighbouring slopes by the shore, thither the octopus's mind is drawn, as upon a scent the keen-nosed Knossian hound's strength is drawn, who in the mountains tracks the beast, searching out its winding path by the unerring message of its nose, and swiftly it seizes the beast and does not fail, but brings it near its master; so too the octopus straightway perceives the flourishing olive near, and emerges from the depths and creeps up the land exulting, and draws near the trunks of Athena; there first, rejoicing about the root, it wreathes the lower stem, winding round like a boy who welcomes his nurse newly come to him, and twines about her, and lifts his hands to her bosom, longing to clasp her neck and throat; so it wreathes about the trunk, rejoicing in the tree. Thence, propping itself on its outermost suckers, it climbs upward eagerly, and about the foliage it folds itself, holding now this branch, now that, as some man returned from abroad greets his comrades, who come thronging to meet him, twining about his neck; or as the moist coil of ivy winds about the tall fir-trees, and stretching from its root it creeps, and flows all round with its tendrils; so it, rejoicing, wraps the sleek shoots of the olive, like one kissing; but when of its love it has its fill, again it creeps back to the bosom of the sea, sated with affection and with longing for the olive. By this very love its capture comes, as the fishers learned; for binding together olive shoots, the most well-grown, they set lead in the midst, and trail them from the boat; and the octopus, perceiving, did not neglect them, but darted and twined about its dear branches; nor thereafter, even while drawn to capture, does it loose the bonds of longing, until it comes within the boat; nor did it hate the olive, even while perishing.

The sargues set their heart on love of goats, and long for goats, and in the mountain-bred herds they take exceeding joy, sea-creatures though they are. A wonder past belief, that kindred tribes were born loving each other—the crags of the mountains and the grey sea. For when the goatherds drive their bleating flocks to the shore-line, to bathe in the salt eddies at noon, when the burning Olympian star stands high, then the sargues, hearing the bleating by the shore and the deep-toned cry of the goat-herds, all together, sluggish though they are, come hurrying borne along, and leap upon the sea's high banks, rejoicing, and fawn about the horned company and lick about them and pour round in a throng, leaping thick; and wonder holds the herdsmen who first behold it; and the goats not unwilling receive their dear chorus; and no satiety of joy holds the fish. Not so much in the covered folds of the shepherds do the kids, exulting from pasture, receive their mothers with much gladness and friendliness, when all the place around rings with the joyful cries of the little ones, and the herdsmen's mind laughs, as those press about the horned herds. But when they have had their fill of the sea-bathing, and the goats go back again to their pens, then the sargues, grieving, all together follow close, where the laughter of the topmost wave passes into the land. As when a mother sends forth her cherished son, or a wife her husband, going to a foreign land far off, grieving, and her mind frets within, how great the stretch of sea between, how many the rounds of months; and stepping upon the topmost waves of the sea she sends a tearful cry from her lips, beseeching him to hasten, and her feet no longer bear her back as she yearns, but she holds her gaze upon the deep; so for these one might say the tears drop from their eyes, left lonely when the goats are driven away. Poor sargue! for soon, I say, an evil love for the goats will fall upon you; such a mind in the anglers turned your loves toward deceit and doom. First the man marks those rocks near the land that rise close together with twin crests, which hold a narrow strait of sea between, bright with the rays of heaven, in which many sargues dwell, having a common-built home; for they rejoice exceedingly in the fires of the sun. There a man, casting a goat-skin over his limbs, fastening two horns about his own temples, sets out, plotting a shepherd's wile, and casts into the sea barley-meal greased with goat-flesh and savour; and the dear smell and the deceitful sight and the well-given food draw them on, nor do they think of any ruin in their hearts, but rejoicing they remain, fawning about the man-foe who resembles a goat; poor wretches, how then they meet a deadly comrade, not knit of goat-nature! For at once against them he arms a stout rod and a line of grey flax, and casts over the hook flesh native to a goat's hoof; and they snatch the food eagerly, and he draws with his thick hand, hauling back; for if any suspect the work of deceit, they would no longer come near, even if he should bring the very shaggy-haired goats, but they flee, loathing all together both the shape and the feast and the very haunts of the rock; but if he escape notice and ply his swift toil, none of the catch would be left, but the goat's look will overcome them all.

Another longing too belongs to the sargues in the season of spring, for one another, and over bed and marriage they contend; one fights for many mates, and whoever in might conquers becomes the husband sufficient for all, and drives the female troop to the rocks; there the fishers have contrived a deep creel, rounded on every side; and they cover all the mouth round with the foliage of plants, of myrtle or fragrant laurel or some other, shading it skilfully with leafy sprigs. The sting drives the suitors on to battle, to fight, and a great bridal War of Enyo arises. But when one, proving best, takes the mastery, at once a smooth rock he scans, a home for his brides, and sees the creel lying there, roofed over with leafy boughs, and there he drives his bridal chorus; and they then sink into the creel, while he outside keeps off all the males, nor lets any other approach the brides. But when he has filled the woven snare, last of all himself he thrust into the chamber, the bed of Hades from which is no return. As when a shepherd, driving from pasture his wool-bearing flocks, leads them home again, and in the doorway standing of the fold he counts in his mind the throng of sheep, ordering them well, whether all are safe for him, and as the flocks press in, the courtyard, filled to overflowing, is crowded, and last among them the shepherd hastened in; so the females first went down into the hollow recess, and last the husband leaped in after, wretched, hastening with his wretched brides. Such are the contests love set up among the fish, and by such love-mad deceits they perished.

The dolphin-fish, when they spy something drifting amid the waves, all in a throng follow close near it; and most of all when a storm-shattered ship, struck by the dread wrath of pitiless Poseidon, and the great wave, dividing it, bears the timbers this way and that, loosed in many fragments. Then the schools of dolphin-fish, following the floating planks, pursue them; and the man who meets with such fishers easily takes a great and unenvied catch. But may the Son of Cronus in the deep keep this from sailors, and may the ships run through the broad wave on gentle breezes, unharmed and unshaken, going about their cargo with toils exchanged in turn; but for the dolphin-fish other devices must be contrived, and without harm to ships their capture won. Binding bundles of reeds together, they set them in the eddies, and below tie a heavy stone as anchor; and all these in the water they whirl quietly; and at once the shade-loving tribes of dolphin-fish gather in a school, and about their backs, delighting in the reeds, they rub themselves, lingering; then the fishers sail upon them for the ready catch, and arming their hooks with baits they send them out; and the fish draw them, hastening their own death. As when a man stirs dogs to a struggle with food, whirling among them the morsels, and they, upon their bellies raging exceedingly, outstrip one another with snatching frenzy, racing past each other and peering at the hand of the man, where he may throw it, and strife of teeth appears; so do these dart readily upon the hooks. Easily you will draw one captive after another, being swift; for they themselves hasten more than the fishers, in their folly speeding their own doom. By such cunning too the pilot-fish is caught; for in them too the heart is alike set on shady loves.

For the squid let a man devise a spindle, fashioning it just like a distaff; and about it let him fasten thickly, bending back the barbs, hooks close beside one another, on which he should pierce the dappled body of a rainbow-wrasse, hiding the upturned bites of the bronze, and in the grey depths of the sea fastening such a snare let him trail it; and the squid, seeing it, darts forth, and clasping it presses with its moist fringes, and is pinned upon the lips of bronze; nor any longer, though it would, can it let go, but unwilling it is drawn, its own self-woven body wrapped about it.

And one too in the unbuffeted harbours of the sea contrived a catching of eels, a boy at play. Taking a sheep's gut of great length, he let it down through the water stretched out, like a long line; and the eel, seeing it, rushed and seized it; and as it gaped he knew it, and at once arched the sheep's-gut with a breath, breathing into the entrail; and it rises with violent gasping, swollen, and fills the stretched mouth of the wretched eel; and it groans, labouring beneath the breath of the man, and is bound though it longs to escape, until, swelling and gasping past restraint, it floats upward and comes into the hunter's hands. As when one, testing a full wine-jar, holding a tube, presses the blow-pipe to his mouth, and with his breath draws back the wine's draught, sucking it up with his outermost lips, and it runs up at the man's breath; so the eels, surging up beneath the breath, are drawn toward the mouth of the deceitful blow-pipe.

There is a wretched and feeble crowd of fish, the close-thronging brood of the weak anchovy, which are called sprats; good food they are for all fishes; and ever in their hearts panic is kindled, and they tremble at everything, and poured together they remain heaped in a mass and grow fast together in a throng, as if bearing the force of a constraining bond; nor could you devise a parting of the wide swarm nor a loosening; so fast do they hold to one another. Often even ships, as upon reefs, have run aground on them, and often the oarsmen of the rowlocks strike them with their oars, and the blade, eager though it is, is held fast, as though it had struck a rocky shoal; and someone, lifting straight up a heavy-mouthed axe, struck the sprats, and did not cleave the whole mass with the iron, but divided off a small portion of the school; and of this it cut off the head, and that it docked of its tail, and that it mowed in the middle, and another it took whole. A piteous sight, bodies like wretched corpses. Yet not even so did they forget, nor did they let go their bond; such a rivet holds them together. And one might gather with his hands, as if meeting deep sand, those very fish, heaping them up. When the fishers mark them crouching upon one another, they wrap them round in the hollow seines gladly, and bring a great catch to the shores without toil, and all their vessels they filled with sprats, and loaded the boats, and on the deep shores they heaped up piles, an endless flood of catch. As when the labourers of Deo, when they have done their work and winnowed the grain by the wind and by hand-oars, have piled up much in the midst of the well-rolled threshing-floor, and all round the grain-receiving rim of the threshing-floor grows white, filled to overflowing within; so then, filled to the brim with countless sprats, the brow of the sea-neighbouring beach grows white.

The tribes of the bonito are by birth from the Euxine sea, the children of the heavy-minded tunny; for those, where the Maeotic lake mingles with the brine, gathering at the marsh's mouth and the watery reed-beds, bethought them of their painful labour of birth; and whatever eggs they find as they course along they devour, but those that remain among the reeds and the rushes bring forth schools of bonito in their season; and these, when first they brush the wave and make trial of the passage, hasten on a strange voyage of the sea, nor will they remain where they were born, small though they are.

There is a certain passage of the Thracian sea, which men say is the deepest, set in Poseidon's allotments; from this it is even called the Black, nor do violent or overstrong winds leap upon it too much; and in it there are hollow recesses below the surface, muddy, unspeakable, in which much is bred that gives feasts to the small fishes. There too for the new-born schools of bonito lie their first paths, since beyond all other sea-creatures they shudder at the ill-blowing onset of winter; and winter dulls the light of the bonito's eyes. There, fallen into the broad flanks of the sea, they simply linger, and growing they await the gentle spring; and then too the desire of the bed comes upon them; and filled with offspring they speed back again to their fathers' wave, having put from their womb their labour. These over the deep gulf of the Black passage the Thracians hunt in the cruel season of winter, a grievous and joyless hunt, beneath the bloody ordinance of war and the savage fate of slaughter. There is a beam not long but as thick as may be, its length a cubit, a stout stake; and at its tip is much poured lead, and many barbs of iron, three-pronged, set close together; and a very long well-plaited cable goes about it. Sailing out with the spar where the sea's passage is deepest, into the misty depth they sent the mighty mass down below with full force from the fir-built keel; and at once with a rush, speeding, weighed down by lead and iron, it darts to the nethermost roots of the sea, where upon the feeble bonito, crouching in the slime, it fell; it took and pierced as many of the wretched throng as it reached. And swiftly they drew them up, driven through with the bronze, quivering piteously with the iron's pains. And one beholding them, even a stout-hearted man, would pity the ill-caught hunt and their fate; for of one the spear-point was driven through the flanks, and of another the swift shaft pierced the head, and one above the tail is wounded, and the belly of another, and another's back the bitter War took, and another is run through the middle of the flank. As when, the warrior tumult decided, men gather up from the dust and blood the spear-slain and send them to the fiery bed, their own comrades mourning; and many and varied upon the corpses' bodies are the wounds, and the shafts of War crowd thick; so upon the bonito too the wounds appear everywhere, an image of war, dear though to the fishers.

Others again with light nets take the tribes of the feeble bonito; for ever in the darkness, whatever falls upon the brine, they tremble, and hold a dread of the gloom; in the gloom they are hunted, terrified throughout the deep. For setting very light nets of thin flax they whirl them round in a circle, striking with force of oars the back of the sea, and with poles they clatter down upon it; and the fish, under the swift-oared flashing and the din, in panic leap, and into the bosom of the net they go, which stands still, thinking it a shelter, foolish ones, who in fear of the noise crossed into death. Then the men press on with the ropes on either side, drawing the net to the shores; and the fish, seeing the ropes moving, holding empty terrors, huddle together and cower and are coiled in a throng. Many a prayer might the net-caster then make to the hunting gods, that nothing leap outside the flax, nor anything stir to show the way; for if the bonito see it, swiftly all over the light flax they dart to the deep and leave the catch unaccomplished. But if none of the sea-roaming blessed ones grudge them, often even dragged over the dry shore, out of the water, they will not leave the net, but cling fast, shuddering at the much-coiling cord itself. So too in the thickets the mountain hunters take the strengthless herd of deer by their lucky craft, wreathing the whole copse with cord; and about it they bind the swift feathers of light birds; and the deer, seeing them, crouch in vain with empty fear, nor do they desire idly to draw near, terrified by the feathers, until the hunters, darting upon them, take them.

And one too, a diver skilled in works of the sea, without a snare, with his hands darting upon them, took the very fish, as though crossing a passage of land instead of brine, both the sargue that trembles in fear and the timid corb. The sargues, in their terror, all in a throng into the recess of the sea huddle and cower, and are poured upon one another, falling sidelong, and bristle up with their spines, bending back their backs, as with stakes on every side the husbandmen fence the running fence of the threshing-floor with thick thorns, a great trouble to the ravagers; nor could anyone enter; for the stakes bar the ways; so one would not readily come near these, nor lay a hand on them; for the dark thorns bristle round in rows, close-set, beneath their points. But let a man by his knowledge dive swiftly beneath the depths of the deep, and mark out on every side the sargues, where their head is and where their tail-set; and casting his hand over their heads, the spines from above let him gently stroke and press them down, bending them; and they stay just as they are, knit together, unmoved, trusting in their sharp defences; then the man, lifting two in his hands on either side, sails up again, having accomplished a most thievish work.

But when fear enters the heart of the rock-haunting corb, swiftly it rushes upon the reefs, and into some hollow hole it enters, a recess running round, or a cleft, or it runs beneath the sea-weeds, or beneath the moist wrack; for it cares not for a shelter such as might receive and save the whole of it, but its head alone it seeks to fence, and hiding its head and eyes it hopes, not seeing, to escape the watcher's onset. As when, with the ravening lion rushing upon her, an antelope in the thickets, turning down her head, sets up a vain defence, nor does she hope to be seen, until the deadly beast, darting upon her, tears her; and like is the corb's heart, nor does it incline its head, but thinks, even while perishing, to escape. Such tricks too the winged crook-necked creature of Libya foolishly devises; and its craft proved vain; so the tender corb, by feeble hopes, hides; for soon, having dragged it up with his hands, the hunter rose and revealed it in its folly.

So much I have learned of the sea-working craft's designs of the fishers, and the bitter doom upon so many fishes; but all the others alike a common fate o'ertakes, of creels and hooks and the deep-woven net and the cast of the trident, all the gear of men's craft. Some the dawn took overcome, others the evening, when at the first gloom of night the fishers, kindling a torch and steering the hollow boat, bring an unseen doom upon the unwary fish. There some, exulting in the bright flame of pine, rush about the boat, and saw an evil evening fire, meeting the cast of the pitiless trident.

There is yet another mode of the hunt for fish-striking poisoners, who devised a baleful poison against the fish, and set a swift-fated end upon the creatures. First with crowded missiles and casts of poles and battering of oars they herd the wretched ranks of the fish into one place, hollow-formed, broken by frequent caverns; there some sink beneath the hollow reefs, and the men set all round the well-fencing nets of flax in a circle, as against hostile men casting about them a double, unfriendly wall of rock. And then the man, lifting up at once rich potter's clay and a root, which the healers have named cyclamen, mixing them in his hands, kneaded two cakes; and into the sea above the nets he leaped, and about those very hollows and chambers he smeared the ill-breathing drugs of the hateful unguent, and defiled the sea. And the man who poured the deadly poison the ship received back again; and the fish at once an evil and hostile smell first reaches in their chambers; and with mist their eyes and head and limbs grow heavy, nor can they remain in the recesses, but in terror they pour out from the reefs; and the sea about them is far more bitter; such a bane is mingled in the waves. And they, like men heavy with wine, drunk on the deadly breath, whirl everywhere and nowhere have a place left free of the evil, and rushing upon the nets in haste they fall, eager to leap through; but there is no release from the harsh ruin, no escape; with much rushing and leaping they surge, tormented; and over Amphitrite spreads the great gasping of the dying, which to the wretched fish became a wail; while outside, the fishers in their pains take pleasure and remain at ease, until silence takes the sea, and from the surge and the grievous tumult they cease, breathing out their groaning last breath. And then they draw up the countless throng of corpses, dead together in a common, defiling doom. As when men set War against their enemies, longing to lay waste a city utterly, and they do not slacken, plotting woes against them, but even the water of the springs they poisoned with destruction; and the people upon the towers, toiling with grievous famine and misery and the hateful water, by a loathsome and shameful death perish, and the whole city is filled with corpses; so these by a deadly fate and a bitter doom, overcome by the poisoning men, were destroyed.

From this, then, hearing, judge, O lord of the land, that nothing is impossible for mortals, neither on earth their mother to labour, nor through the dank bosom of the sea; but truly some one brought forth a race like the blessed gods, even men, and gave them a lesser strength, whether the offspring of Iapetus, Prometheus of many counsels, fashioned a race to face the blessed ones, joining earth to water, and anointed their heart with the gods' own ointment, or whether we are sprung from the god-flowing gore of the Titans; for nothing is mightier than men apart from the gods; to the immortals alone we yield. For how many beasts upon the mountains, holding unflinching might, overweening creatures, has mortal man quenched! And how many tribes of birds, wheeling in the clouds and the air, has he taken, though his own frame keeps low to the ground! Nor did the lion's pride save it from being tamed, nor did the windy rush of his wings save the eagle, but even the Indian black-hided beast, that overweening burden, by force they bowed, pressing upon it, and set it under the yoke of mules to bear the patient toil of a draught-hauler. And as for the monsters, vast as they are, that in Poseidon's haunts are reared, I say the sea breeds these no less savage than the flesh-eating offspring of the land, but in strength too and in size they surpass them, the shameless terrors of the deep. There is a kind of land-tortoise, and they know no might nor any harm; but with the sea-turtle not very boldly will any man meet in the waves. On the dry land there are fierce dogs, yet with the dogs of the sea no man could vie in shamelessness. The leopard is a deadly bane of the land, but the sea's is more dreadful. Over the dry land walk the hyenas, but far more chilling are those in the surge. There are rams, the tame flock of shepherds, but with the ram of the sea no gentleness will he meet who comes near it. Who carries strength so great as the boar, as the invincible lamnae carry? Whose heart blazes with a lion's might, that could match the shuddersome hammerhead-sharks? The grim seal even on land the long-haired bears shudder at, and meeting it in battle are overcome; in such beasts does the sea delight. But for all that, against these too the burdensome ruin the unconquerable race of men of a day devised, and by the fishers they are destroyed, when they rush into battle with the monsters. Of their hunting I will tell the heavy toil; but hear me, gracious kings, Olympian walls of the land.

Monsters are reared in the mid-flowing seas, most numerous and most vast; and they do not rise from the brine often, but below they keep the floor of the sea by their weight, and rave with the ceaseless frenzy of hunger, ever famished and never from their dread belly loosing their greed; for what food shall be so great as to fill the chaos of their gut, as to lull to surfeit that invincible jaw? And they too destroy one another, the stronger slaying the weaker in might, and to one another are food and feasts. Often too they bring terror, encountering ships on the western Iberian sea, where most of all the neighbouring Ocean's unspeakable water, left behind, gathers, like ships of twenty oars. Often too, wandering, it comes near the shore of deep waters, when one might arm against it. For all the monstrous beasts of the sea, save the dogs, the ways are heavy-limbed and not easily plied; for they neither see from afar nor traverse the whole sea, weighed down by their towering limbs, but very late, rolling, are they borne along. Therefore a fish goes as fellow-traveller with all of them, grey to look upon and long of body, with a slender tail, which above all leads the way of the sea before them, giving signs; and for this they have named it the Guide. To the monster it is an exceedingly welcome comrade, an escort and a guard; and it carries the monster where it will easily; for that one alone the fish follows, keeping a faithful mind ever toward a faithful friend; and near it it turns about, and stretches close before its eyes its tail, which makes plain to it each thing—whether there is some prey to take, or whether some bane is mustering near, or whether the spread of sea is shallow, which it is better to shun; and as if it spoke, the tail shows all things most truly; and the burden of water obeys it. For that fish is the monster's champion and its ears and its light; to it the monster listens, by it it sees, having entrusted to it the keeping of its own life. As a child cherishes his aged father, repaying the nurture with cares that tend his age, and now, when his limbs and eyes have grown feeble, attending him kindly, embraces him, and on the roads holds out his hand, and in all his works himself defends him; for to an aging father his sons are new strength; so that fish in love embraces the bane of the sea, guiding it like a ship by helm and rein. Surely from its first birth a kindred blood fell to it, or it took the monster itself and made it comrade of its heart. So neither of manhood nor of beauty is there profit so great as of wits; and might without sense is foolish; and a small but cunning man has quenched and saved himself from one greatly mighty; since even the invincible monster, of unapproachable limbs, sets before it a little fish. Therefore let one take first as his target that Guide, beguiling it by the hook's force and by a bait; for you could not, pressing upon it while it lives, master the beast, but once it is gone its ruin will be the swifter. For it no longer knows truly the ways of the violet-dark brine, nor how to shun a bane close at hand, but simply, like a merchant-ship whose steersman has perished, it drifts unguarded, helpless, wherever the grey water may drive it, and through dark and trackless passages it is borne, bereft of its helping charioteer. Often too it runs aground on rocks and on shores, drifting; such a mist is spread over its eyes. Then indeed with eager designs to the toil of the hunt the fishers hasten, having prayed to the blessed ones, the slayers of monsters, to take the grievous portent of Amphitrite. As when a strong band of enemies draws stealthily near their foes, watching for midnight, and finds the watchmen asleep before the gates, with War's favour, and falling on them overcomes them; thence then upon the citadel and the very tower boldly they press, bearing the fire-bolt, the city's ruin, the brand that shatters the well-built halls; so then boldly the host of fishers presses on after the unfenced beast, its steersman slain. First in their minds they reckon its weight and its size; and these are the signs from its limbs: if, as it rolls amid the eddies of the deep, it lifts up a little of its ridge and the gleaming top of its crest, then it is great and surpassing; for not even the very sea bears it easily, heaving it up; but if any of its back shows, it announces not so great a weight; for the ways are light for the feebler ones. For these the line is fitted with close-set joinings of many twisted cords, as great as the forestay of a ship neither deep nor small; and its length is stretched out sufficient for the prey; and the well-wrought hook is notched with alternating projections of barbs, sharpened on both sides, such as could grip a rock and pierce a crag, so great a curve of metal, that might cover round the gape. A twisted chain is set about the end of the dark hook, stout, bronze-forged, which the savage force of teeth might withstand, and the points of the jaws; and in the middle of the bond round wheel-like rings are made, close beside one another, to keep off the wild twistings, lest it break straight off the iron, bleeding, racked with deadly pains, but instead let it wind in a wheeling, wandering course. On the hook they make ready a grim feast, the black liver of a bull, set apart, or the raw flesh of a bull, like the jaws of a beast that feeds. And many, as fellow-marchers with the fishers as if to war, are whetted: strong points and stout tridents, sickles and heavy-mouthed axes, and all such shattering tools as are forged on the loud-clanging anvils. Swiftly, mounting the well-benched boats, silently nodding to one another what need there is, they set out, and with quiet oars the sea softly they whiten, guarding against any noise, lest the great monster learn of it and, shunning them, go down to the depths beneath the waves, and they reap their toil in vain. But when they draw near it and join battle in the contest, then boldly from the prow against the monstrous beast they cast the bane of the snare; and it, when it saw the heavy feast, leaped, and did not neglect it, trusting its shameless belly; and rushing on it seized the curved doom, and at once within the sharpened hook sank into its wide gullet, and was fixed in the barbs; and the beast, its heart stirred by the wound, first, fretting, tosses its deadly jaw against it, striving to break the bronze cord; but its toil is spent in vain; and thereafter, speeding, weighed down by fiery pains, it sinks into the gulfs beneath the waves of the sea; and the fishers at once let out to it all the line; for there is not strength in men to draw up and to master, while it refuses, the heavy monster; for easily, deck-timbers and all, it would drag the ships to the depths, when it sets out to rush away. But to it, as it sinks, they send broad skins fastened to the line, filled with human breath, straight into the water; and it, fretting with pains, heeds not the skins, and easily dragged them down, unwilling, longing for the topmost foam of the sea. But when it draws near the bottom with weary heart, it stands, foaming greatly, downcast; and as a horse that has run out his toilsome sweat to the very goal grinds his jaw under the bloody foam upon the crooked bit, and the hot panting spreads through his mouth, so the monster, gasping greatly, takes its rest, nor do the skins allow it, though it longs, to remain below, but swiftly they speed upward and dart out of the brine, lifted by the breath; and for it another contest stands. Then first it darts with its jaws a vain rush, eager to ward off the skins that drag it; but they fly up, nor do they wait for it, fleeing like living things that escape; and it, fretting, makes for the inmost brine again, and winds in many a twisting, now by constraint, now of its own will, drawing and drawn back in turn. As when timber-cutters labour at a common toil, plying the saw busily, when a keel or some other need they hasten to accomplish for seafarers, and both, with the rough iron pressed home, draw back its strength, nor ever does the file of teeth turn one way, but, hurrying from either side, it grates and saws and is drawn back ever again; such is the strife of the skins and the bloody beast, the one hauled up, the others forcing it from the other side.
